title: Ten Feet Down
subtitle: A 9-year-old boy after a treehouse fall — pain, deformity, and a head to toe problem

presentation.report: Medic 7 rolling in with Andres Villanueva, 9-year-old male, unrestrained fall approximately 10 feet from a treehouse onto mixed grass and dirt. He was found upright and crying at the scene. GCS was 14 at the scene, he opened eyes spontaneously, was confused and repeating himself, and withdrew to pain — he's improved to 14-15 en route and now he's verbally appropriate but still confused about what day it is. We collared him in the field for mechanism. Obvious angulated deformity of the left mid-forearm — we splinted it in place. Scalp lac over the left parietal region, actively bled at scene; we applied a pressure dressing and it's slowed way down. IV is in the right antecubital, 18-gauge, patent — no fluids hung yet. VS en route: HR 118, RR 22, BP 104/66, SpO2 97% on room air.
presentation.learnMore: Falls from height are the leading mechanism of pediatric trauma in the school-age group. A 10-foot fall carries enough kinetic energy to produce TBI, long-bone fractures, solid organ injury, and pneumothorax — even when the child appears to have 'landed okay.' The initial exam can dramatically underestimate injury burden; systematic primary and secondary surveys with low thresholds for imaging are the standard of care. Cervical spine injury after pediatric falls is uncommon but cannot be cleared clinically in a child who is confused or has distracting pain.

phases.title: Primary Survey
phases.narrative: Andres arrives on the EMS stretcher, collar in place with a blood-spotted head bandage over the left parietal scalp laceration. He's awake and crying, calling for his mom, and answers questions appropriately though he keeps asking 'what happened' — he's lost about 30 minutes. He's moving all four extremities but guarding his left forearm, which has an obvious mid-shaft angulation with intact skin. The right antecubital 18-gauge IV is secured and patent. Breath sounds are equal and clear bilaterally, trachea is midline, and his abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness on palpation — no rigidity, no guarding. Peripheral pulses are present but slightly diminished at the left wrist distal to the deformity; radial pulse is intact on the right.

vitals.label: Heart Rate
vitals.why:
At 9 years old, Andres's heart rate of 122 bpm is at the upper edge of normal — the healthy range at his age tops out around 118 — but in the context of his trauma picture, this is compensatory tachycardia masking ongoing blood loss. His blood pressure still looks reassuring, but that's exactly the trap: kids hold their BP by racing their heart much longer than adults do, and by the time his pressure drops, he's already lost a dangerous amount of volume.

- **Sympathetic activation** in response to blood loss triggers catecholamine release (his body's own adrenaline), which speeds the heart and constricts peripheral vessels to maintain central perfusion — that's why his cap refill is already slow at 3 seconds despite a normal-range BP.
- **Hemoglobin of 11.2 with a cap refill delay and mild lactate elevation** confirms he's bleeding and compensating: the low hemoglobin shows blood loss, the sluggish cap refill shows peripheral vasoconstriction to preserve core blood pressure, and the rising lactate signals tissues are not getting enough oxygen despite the fast heart rate.

Keep reassessing his heart rate every few minutes and his perfusion signs closely — if the tachycardia worsens or his cap refill lengthens further, that's your signal he's decompensating and needs urgent fluid resuscitation and imaging to find the bleeding source.

vitals.label: Resp Rate
vitals.why:
Andres's respiratory rate of 22 is right at the upper limit of normal for a 9-year-old, which is reassuring — he's not compensating hard for tissue hypoxia or metabolic acidosis yet. But in the context of his trauma picture, a normal respiratory rate sits alongside concerning perfusion signs: cap refill of 3 seconds, tachycardia of 122, and a lactate of 2.6 that signals tissue hypoperfusion despite a normal blood pressure. His breathing isn't fast, but his body is already compensating through the cardiac and metabolic channels.

- **Compensatory tachycardia without tachypnea** suggests his shock is not respiratory in origin and his oxygenation is intact — his lungs are doing their job, so the hypoperfusion isn't driving a respiratory response yet.
- **Lactate elevation with normal pCO2** means the metabolic acidosis is mild enough that respiratory compensation isn't kicking in; if shock deepens, watch for Kussmaul-pattern breathing as the body tries to blow off the accumulated acid.

Recheck respiratory rate in 15 minutes: if it climbs above 28–30 while cap refill stays prolonged, that signals worsening tissue debt and need for more aggressive resuscitation.

vitals.label: Blood Pressure
vitals.why:
Andres's blood pressure of 102/64 is normal for a 9-year-old by the numbers, but it sits in a dangerous gray zone: he is bleeding (low hemoglobin and hematocrit), his heart is racing at 122, his cap refill is 3 seconds, and his lactate is elevated at 2.6 — all signs he is compensating hard to keep that pressure up. Once you see this combination, a "normal" BP is actually a red flag, not reassurance.

- **Compensated shock** in children is deceptive because kids maintain systolic pressure through rapid heart rate and intense vasoconstriction long after adults would have dropped. His tachycardia and sluggish perfusion (cap refill 3 sec) are the body's emergency response to blood loss; the normal BP is the result, not evidence he is stable.
- **Lactate of 2.6 with intact perfusion organs** suggests tissue hypoperfusion is already present — his cells are working anaerobically despite a blood pressure number that looks reassuring on paper.

Watch his trend: if the heart rate does not come down or cap refill does not improve after initial fluid resuscitation and control of bleeding, his BP will drop precipitously. That is when decompensation becomes obvious — but by then time is running out.

vitals.label: SpO2
vitals.why:
SpO2 of 97% is reassuring because it tells you Andres's airway is patent and his lungs are moving air effectively — the trauma hasn't triggered respiratory compromise yet. But oxygenation alone doesn't mean he's perfusing well; his fast heart rate, slow capillary refill, and elevated lactate tell a different story underneath a normal oxygen level.

- **Normal SpO2 in trauma masks hypoperfusion.** Andres can oxygenate his blood just fine, but his heart rate of 122 and cap refill of 3 seconds show his tissues aren't receiving what his lungs are delivering — this is the hallmark of shock compensating with speed rather than with visible cyanosis.
- **Lactate of 2.6 with normal oxygenation flags anaerobic metabolism from blood loss, not lung failure.** The bleeding from his head wound, the angulated forearm fracture, and the mild abdominal tenderness suggest occult volume loss; his body is running on fumes despite pink oxygen numbers.

Keep SpO2 on the monitor, but don't let a reassuring value distract you — this child needs volume resuscitation now because shock doesn't always announce itself with low oxygen.

vitals.label: Temperature
vitals.why:
Andres's temperature of 37.1°C is normal, and that's reassuring in the immediate hours after trauma — but it doesn't mean he's safe from internal bleeding. After blunt head and abdominal trauma, a normal temp tells you the hypothermia that signals severe shock hasn't arrived yet; it doesn't rule out ongoing blood loss into the belly or intracranial space. Watch the trend, not the single number.

- **Shock progression in pediatric trauma follows a heat-to-cold arc.** Early compensatory shock can maintain core temperature while peripheral perfusion collapses — his cap refill of 3 seconds and borderline-elevated lactate suggest he's starting that climb, even though his vitals and temperature appear deceptively stable.
- **Hypothermia (<36°C) in trauma signals decompensated shock and poor prognosis.** If his temperature begins to drift downward over the next hour, that's your signal that resuscitation isn't keeping pace with his ongoing losses and he needs escalated intervention.

Recheck temperature with the same serial assessment you're doing for hemoglobin and perfusion markers — a falling temperature is a late but critical warning that compensated shock is breaking down.

vitals.label: Cap Refill
vitals.why:
Capillary refill of 3 seconds is a red flag for shock in a 9-year-old, even though his blood pressure is still normal — this is the moment to recognize that compensation is working but running thin. At 3 seconds, the capillaries are sluggish because his body is squeezing blood away from the skin to protect the heart and brain; it's an early warning that perfusion is starting to fail, not a late finding. In trauma with ongoing bleeding, this matters urgently because the next hour determines whether shock stays compensated or tips into decompensation.

- **Compensated shock maintains blood pressure through tachycardia and vasoconstriction** — Andres's HR of 122 and prolonged cap refill show his body is working hard to keep his BP normal, but those mechanisms have limits and can fail suddenly once enough blood volume is gone.
- **A lactate of 2.6 with borderline perfusion signals tissue hypoxia from inadequate oxygen delivery**, which means his cells are already beginning anaerobic metabolism even while his vital signs look deceptively stable — the lactate confirms what the cap refill hints at.

Reassess cap refill every 15 minutes and watch for any rise in heart rate, any drop in BP, or any dulling of mental status; those are your signals that compensation is breaking down.

signs.label: Mental Status
signs.finding: Alert and crying, verbally appropriate, oriented to person and place but not time or event. Repeating questions about what happened — approximately 30 minutes of retrograde amnesia. GCS 14: eyes open spontaneously (4), confused verbal response (4), obeys commands (6).
signs.why:
Andres's confusion and 30-minute memory gap tell you he has sustained a head injury with altered consciousness — this is a concussion or worse, and the pattern matters more than the single moment you're observing him now. A child who is awake and talking but cannot recall events is not simply "alert"; he has lost a window of time, which signals diffuse axonal disruption or post-traumatic amnesia rather than a focal mass effect.

- **Post-traumatic amnesia** (the inability to form new memories or recall events before impact) is the most sensitive marker of brain injury severity and predicts longer recovery and higher risk of repeat concussion if he returns to activity too soon.
- **GCS 14 with intact pupil reactivity and midline trachea** means no emergent herniation right now, but the combination of tachycardia, delayed cap refill, and borderline-low hemoglobin signals he is compensating for blood loss from scalp and forearm trauma — his brain is still at risk if perfusion declines further.

Watch the mental status closely over the next 30 minutes: improving clarity is reassuring; worsening confusion, vomiting, or lethargy is your sign to escalate imaging and consider ICU admission.

signs.label: Pupils
signs.finding: Pupils 4 mm bilaterally, equal and reactive to light, brisk consensual response. No anisocoria.
signs.why:
Andres's normal pupils tell you his brainstem is intact and there's no focal mass effect pushing the midbrain — a critical reassurance after head trauma with brief loss of consciousness. Pupil reactivity depends on the parasympathetic fibers that travel with the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III), which is exquisitely sensitive to increased intracranial pressure; dilated or sluggish pupils are an early warning that intracranial pressure is rising.

- **Intact pupillary light reflex** means the pathway from retina through the brainstem to the parasympathetic motor fibers is working — this rules out the most immediately dangerous forms of traumatic brain injury (epidural hematoma with uncal herniation, diffuse axonal injury with brainstem involvement).
- **Anisocoria or sluggishness** would signal compression of CN III and demand urgent CT and neurosurgery evaluation; the absence of either in a child with posttraumatic amnesia keeps the clinical picture in the realm of mild-to-moderate concussion rather than neurosurgical emergency.

Keep reassessing pupils every 15 minutes — change from reactive to sluggish, or development of anisocoria, is your trigger to escalate imaging or neurosurgery consultation immediately.

signs.label: Breath Sounds
signs.finding: Equal and clear to auscultation bilaterally. No wheeze, stridor, or decreased entry. Trachea midline.
signs.why:
Equal and clear breath sounds with midline trachea are reassuring because they tell you Andres's airway is patent and his lungs are ventilating symmetrically — critical facts in any trauma, especially when head injury and shock are present. In a 9-year-old who is crying and alert, you want to hear exactly what you're hearing: no asymmetry (which would suggest pneumothorax or hemothorax from blunt chest trauma), no stridor (which would flag airway compromise from swelling), and no wheezing (which would suggest aspiration or primary pulmonary injury).

- **Patent airway with symmetric ventilation** means you do not need to intervene on the airway right now, so you can focus on resuscitation — the bleeding and shock physiology driving his tachycardia, elevated lactate, and borderline perfusion.
- **Trachea midline** excludes tension pneumothorax, which would shift the trachea and is a life threat requiring needle decompression; its absence removes that diagnosis from your immediate threat list.

Keep reassessing: trauma patients can develop tension physiology minutes after arrival, so listen again if his work of breathing rises or his blood pressure drops.

signs.label: Left Forearm
signs.finding: Mid-shaft angulated deformity with mild swelling. Skin intact, no open wound. Splinted in position by EMS. Sensation reduced over dorsal web space of thumb.
signs.why:
The angulated mid-shaft deformity with a diminished distal pulse signals an unstable both-bones forearm fracture with potential vascular compromise — the immediate priority is splinting to prevent further displacement and urgent vascular reassessment. The scenario describes intact skin with no neurosensory deficit specified in the narrative, so the clinical focus is on the vascular finding rather than a specific nerve injury pattern.

- **Fracture angulation can kink or compress the radial artery**, reducing distal perfusion to the hand; a palpable but diminished left wrist pulse demands urgent and repeated reassessment because complete occlusion can lead to hand ischemia within hours.
- **Splint in the position of function**, keep the limb immobilized at or below heart level, and obtain orthopedic consultation and plain films promptly — if the pulse weakens further or the hand becomes pale and cool, emergent reduction is indicated before imaging.

signs.label: Distal Pulse — Left
signs.finding: Radial pulse palpable but diminished at the left wrist compared to the right. Capillary refill at the left fingertips is 4 seconds.
signs.why:
The diminished pulse at the left wrist tells you the angulated forearm fracture is reducing arterial flow to the hand — this is vascular compromise from local bone displacement, not from systemic shock (his right-sided pulses and blood pressure remain age-appropriate). Urgent orthopedic evaluation and splinting are needed to prevent progression to complete occlusion.

- **Arterial compression from bone angulation** reduces perfusion pressure distal to the injury: the artery is kinked or squeezed by the displaced fracture fragments, dropping flow to the hand even while central hemodynamics remain compensated.
- **Tissue ischemia develops quickly in a limb** — muscle and nerve tolerate only 4–6 hours of complete ischemia before irreversible damage begins, so a diminished-but-present pulse is your signal that the fracture needs orthopedic reduction promptly.

Check the left hand repeatedly: if the pulse disappears or the hand becomes cold and pale, that is emergent — notify orthopedics immediately or prepare for emergency bedside reduction.

signs.label: Scalp Laceration
signs.finding: 3–4 cm linear laceration over left parietal scalp, currently covered by EMS pressure dressing. Minimal active bleeding through the dressing. No palpable step-off or skull depression on exam adjacent to the wound.
signs.why:
The scalp bleeds vigorously because the skin is bound tightly to the skull and cannot contract to compress bleeding vessels — even a small laceration can lose blood quickly in a child. This 3–4 cm wound is significant because the scalp's rich blood supply means ongoing ooze through an inadequate dressing can compound volume loss in a trauma patient who already has a low-normal hemoglobin and an elevated lactate.

- **Scalp bleeding is deceptively brisk** because the dermis is adherent to the galea aponeurotica (the tough fascial layer underneath), preventing the normal vascular contraction that slows bleeding in other body regions.
- **The absence of a palpable step-off or skull depression here is reassuring** — it means the trauma force did not create a depressed fracture or underlying brain injury sign, though you must still assume cervical spine injury until cleared and monitor closely for delayed intracranial effects given his persistent anterograde amnesia.

Pressure dressing, hemostasis, and proper irrigation are urgent; do not underestimate what a scalp wound can cost in milliliters per minute.

signs.label: Abdomen
signs.finding: Soft, non-distended, with mild diffuse tenderness to palpation. No rigidity, no guarding, no rebound. Bowel sounds present.
signs.why:
Mild diffuse abdominal tenderness after blunt trauma is a red flag for solid-organ injury even when the exam doesn't show rigidity or guarding — kids with liver or spleen lacerations often look deceptively well at first. Andres's elevated lactate and slightly low hemoglobin already suggest he's lost some blood; the soft, non-rigid belly doesn't rule that out.

- **Solid-organ lacerations (liver, spleen, kidney)** bleed into the peritoneal space silently at first — rigidity and guarding appear later, after enough blood pools to irritate the peritoneum, not when bleeding just started.
- **Lactate elevation without decompensated shock vitals** points to tissue hypoperfusion from blood loss; the abdominal exam alone cannot exclude intra-abdominal hemorrhage, making **eFAST exam and abdominal CT** essential next steps in this trauma evaluation.

Watch serial exams closely and prioritize imaging — this is the child who needs it.

signs.label: Skin / Perfusion
signs.finding: Skin warm and dry centrally. Mild pallor of the extremities. No petechiae, ecchymosis, or other rash. Right wrist cap refill 3 seconds.
signs.why:
At 9 years old with a 3-second capillary refill and mild extremity pallor, Andres is showing early compensated shock — his core is still perfused and warm, but his body is already squeezing blood away from the skin to protect vital organs. This is the critical window where aggressive fluid resuscitation and source control can prevent decompensation.

- **Sympathetic vasoconstriction** narrows skin vessels to redirect cardiac output inward; pallor and delayed cap refill are the visible result of this protective response, not signs that perfusion has already failed.
- **Hypovolemia from blood loss** (scalp laceration, possible intra-abdominal bleeding given the mild tenderness and elevated lactate) triggers catecholamine surge, which maintains his blood pressure at 102/64 by increasing heart rate and peripheral resistance — that tachycardia at 122 and cool extremities are not separate problems, they're the same compensation working.

Watch for the tripwire: if cap refill creeps from 3 toward 4 seconds, or if his mental status shifts from appropriate but distressed to lethargic, he's crossing from compensated into decompensated shock and needs emergent transfusion or operative intervention.

labs.name: Hemoglobin
labs.why:
Andres's hemoglobin of 11.2 is below the normal range for a 9-year-old and signals he has already lost some red cell mass from the trauma — this is your early warning that bleeding is ongoing or has been significant.

- **Acute blood loss lowers hemoglobin by dilution first.** When Andres bleeds, fluid shifts from the interstitium into the vascular space to maintain volume, diluting the remaining red cells before his body can compensate by making more. A hemoglobin drop of 1–2 g/dL within hours after trauma reflects real blood loss, not anemia from chronic disease.

- **Hemoglobin trends matter more than a single value in trauma.** A hemoglobin of 11.2 that stays stable over the next 2–4 hours suggests the bleeding has slowed; a hemoglobin that continues to drop signals ongoing hemorrhage and need for transfusion or emergent source control. Serial checks every 2–4 hours are your window into whether resuscitation is catching up with blood loss.

Watch the repeat hemoglobin closely — if it drops another 1–2 points despite IV access and fluid resuscitation, that's your trigger to escalate toward type-and-cross and transfusion readiness.

labs.name: Hematocrit
labs.why:
Andres's hematocrit of 33% is below the normal range for a 9-year-old, signaling blood loss from his trauma — and the drop matters more than the single number because he's lost about a liter of whole blood volume already. A hematocrit this low in the acute setting tells you he's bled enough to reduce his oxygen-carrying capacity, which is why his heart is racing at 122 to compensate and his cap refill has stretched to 3 seconds despite a normal blood pressure.

- **Acute blood loss** reduces the hemoglobin available to bind oxygen, forcing the heart to pump faster to deliver the same amount of oxygen to tissues — this is why tachycardia and low hematocrit travel together in trauma.
- **Compensated hemorrhagic shock** preserves blood pressure by squeezing peripheral vessels (narrowing cap refill) and racing the heart, masking how much volume is actually gone until the next bleed tips him over — that's why the lactate sits at 2.6, signaling tissue hypoxia from maldistribution even though his systolic BP looks fine.

Type and crossmatch him now and keep the IV running wide open; a 9-year-old can lose 25–30% of blood volume before blood pressure finally falls, which means he may look deceptively stable while being one more bleed away from decompensation.

labs.name: WBC
labs.why:
Andres's WBC of 11.8 is normal for his age and does not point to infection — which is reassuring because his trauma picture (head injury, fractured forearm, mild abdominal tenderness) could trigger an infection workup if labs looked septic. A normal WBC count in pediatric trauma simply reflects the stress response to injury without bacterial invasion; the absence of bandemia (immature band neutrophils) clinches this as straightforward post-traumatic inflammation rather than evolving sepsis.

- **Stress leukocytosis** from catecholamine surge in trauma raises WBC acutely through demargination — the body mobilizes its circulating white cell reserve without infection driving it.
- **Bandemia** (bands >5%) is the more sensitive early marker of bacterial sepsis than total WBC; a normal differential with normal WBC rules out early bacterial infection even in a critically injured child.

Keep the infection workup in reserve — if Andres's mental status worsens or his abdominal exam evolves, revisit the lactate and consider imaging and blood cultures then.

labs.name: Platelets
labs.why:
Andres's platelets are normal — this is reassuring after trauma because it tells you he hasn't started consuming clotting factors in massive hemorrhage yet. Platelets at 218 mean his marrow is responding normally and his clotting machinery is intact so far, even though his hemoglobin is already down to 11.2 and his lactate is elevated at 2.6, signaling early blood loss and tissue hypoperfusion.

- **Thrombocytopenia in trauma** (platelets <150) signals either bone marrow shutdown from massive transfusion or consumption in disseminated intravascular coagulation — a late finding in hemorrhagic shock that usually means the child is already decompensating.
- **Normal platelets with low hemoglobin** tells you the anemia is from blood loss, not from bone marrow failure or chronic disease, and that clot formation is still functioning normally — critical context as you weigh whether this child needs blood products versus IV fluids and close monitoring.

Watch the hemoglobin trend on repeat labs; if it keeps dropping despite fluid resuscitation, that's your signal to escalate toward type and cross or massive transfusion protocol.

labs.name: Sodium
labs.why:
Sodium is normal here, but it's reassuring *because* Andres has already lost blood — a normal sodium in a hemorrhaging child can hide a bigger picture. Sodium stays locked at ~138 mEq/L partly because water and sodium are lost together in bleeding, and partly because the body prioritizes maintaining plasma osmolarity over all else. The real concern is not the sodium value itself but what it masks: his hemoglobin is down to 11.2 and his hematocrit is 33%, both showing acute blood loss, and his lactate is elevated at 2.6 despite a normal blood pressure — that combination signals tissue hypoxia from reduced oxygen carrying capacity, not yet from shock but trending that way.

- **Pseudonormal electrolytes in hemorrhage** mask the severity of blood loss by holding sodium constant even as red cells disappear; don't let a normal sodium lull you into thinking the anemia is mild.
- **Lactate elevation (2.6) paired with normal BP** is the real red flag: his tissues are working harder to extract oxygen from fewer red cells, and that metabolic debt will worsen if bleeding continues or transfusion is delayed.

Watch the lactate on repeat labs — if it climbs past 3 or if the hemoglobin drops further, this child needs blood, not just crystalloid.

labs.name: Glucose
labs.why:
Andres's glucose of 108 mg/dL is reassuringly normal despite significant trauma — his stress response is compensating appropriately without metabolic derangement at this moment. Glucose rises in acute stress when catecholamines and cortisol trigger hepatic glycogenolysis, so a normal value here actually tells you his endocrine system is responding proportionately to injury rather than cycling into hyperglycemia or fuel crisis. Watch the trend on repeat labs: if glucose climbs above 180–200 mg/dL or drops unexpectedly, that signals either ongoing severe stress (poor prognostic sign) or early shock-related metabolic failure — neither is present yet, and his normal glucose supports the impression that perfusion remains marginally intact despite the tachycardia, diminished left radial pulse, and borderline capillary refill.

- **Stress hyperglycemia** in pediatric trauma typically appears when catecholamine surge drives hepatic glucose output; a normal glucose at presentation suggests his acute stress response is not yet maximal.
- **Preserved perfusion to vital organs** is reflected in maintained glucose production and normal renal excretion; a rising or falling glucose trajectory would be a red flag for decompensation.

labs.name: Lactate
labs.why:
Andres's lactate of 2.6 is elevated and signals tissue hypoxia from blood loss — his body is working harder to extract oxygen when delivery is reduced. A normal lactate would reassure you that perfusion is holding; this one tells you he needs close reassessment and likely transfusion.

- **Anaerobic metabolism** occurs when oxygen delivery drops below what tissues need, forcing cells to shift from efficient aerobic pathways to lactate-producing glycolysis, which accumulates in the blood.
- **Hemorrhagic shock compensation** can maintain normal blood pressure through tachycardia and vasoconstriction even as circulating volume shrinks — the lactate rise is an early warning that compensation is being stretched, visible before BP drops.

Watch the trend: a falling lactate after transfusion means the bleeding is controlled and perfusion is recovering; a climbing lactate signals ongoing bleeding or inadequate resuscitation.

labs.name: ALT
labs.why:
ALT of 62 U/L is mildly elevated and reflects hepatic injury from blunt trauma — a red flag that the abdomen absorbed more force than the soft palpation and absence of guarding suggest. Liver and spleen injuries can present deceptively: a child with normal vital signs and a soft belly can still have a significant intra-abdominal bleed evolving over hours.

- **Hepatic contusion or laceration** from blunt force causes hepatocyte damage and enzyme leakage into the bloodstream, raising transaminases within the first few hours post-injury even when the bleeding is contained by the liver capsule.
- **Serial reassessment matters more than a single value.** ALT of 62 today tells you the liver was hit; ALT of 120 tomorrow tells you ongoing or worsening injury, which raises concern for delayed hemorrhage and the need for imaging or ICU monitoring.

Watch for abdominal distension, worsening tenderness, or dropping hemoglobin on repeat labs — these signal active bleeding and a shift in management from observation to intervention.

labs.name: Lipase
labs.why:
Lipase stays normal here, which is reassuring — it tells you the pancreas is not hurt despite the blunt abdominal trauma and mild tenderness Andres has. A normal lipase rules out acute pancreatitis as a complicating injury.

- **Pancreatic injury in blunt trauma** would trigger lipase release into the bloodstream as acinar cells rupture; elevation usually appears within hours of injury.
- **Mild abdominal tenderness without elevated lipase** points toward simple contusion or minor solid-organ trauma rather than pancreatic damage, which carries high morbidity if missed.

This is one piece of reassurance in an otherwise concerning picture — keep monitoring for peritoneal signs and trending the CBC for occult bleeding, but the pancreas looks safe.

phases.title: Stabilize and Survey
phases.narrative: Andres is becoming more agitated with movement and is starting to resist the C-collar, saying his neck 'hurts a little' but he can't tell you if that's new. His left forearm is visibly angulated under the splint — he rates the pain 8/10 and keeps reaching toward the arm with his right hand. The 18-gauge right antecubital IV is patent. No additional IV access has been placed. Given the mechanism, his mildly elevated lactate, abdominal tenderness, and slightly elevated liver enzymes, you're concerned about occult solid organ injury. His trachea remains midline, breath sounds remain equal and clear, and his abdomen has not worsened — no peritoneal signs. Now is the time to connect monitoring, get better vascular access, image, and get ahead of his pain before it drives his tachycardia higher.

vitals.label: Heart Rate
vitals.why:
At 9 years old, Andres's heart rate of 126 is above the normal awake range (75–118 bpm) and is doing exactly what it should: compensating for pain, anxiety, and the metabolic stress of trauma. His blood pressure is still normal-for-age, which means his tachycardia is *working* — it's keeping perfusion adequate while his body responds to injury. This is compensation, not failure, but it is a signal that he needs analgesia and reassurance right now, before the tachycardia climbs further or his perfusion starts to slip.

- **Pain-driven tachycardia** is protective in the immediate post-trauma window; his 8/10 rating and agitation are fueling the heart rate far more than blood loss or shock at this moment. Treating pain directly will drop his heart rate more reliably than anything else you can do.
- **Metabolic acidosis** (pH 7.31, HCO3 18) with normal pCO2 signals his tissues are working harder than his lungs can compensate for — the tachycardia is partly the body's attempt to blow off CO2 faster, and partly the stress response to pain and injury. His slightly diminished distal pulses and trace hematuria hint at the mechanism: occult solid organ injury or internal bleeding is keeping his lactate mildly elevated and his acid-base status just off normal.

Get his pain controlled and his neck cleared so he can relax the guarding posture — reassess the heart rate after analgesia and you'll see it trend down if perfusion is truly intact.

vitals.label: Resp Rate
vitals.why:
Andres's respiratory rate of 24 is elevated for a 9-year-old at rest (normal 18–25), and it's climbing in response to pain and anxiety rather than primary lung disease — his oxygen is fine, his lungs are clear, but his body is working harder because he hurts.

- **Pain-driven tachypnea** is a reflex response: injury signals drive both heart rate and breathing rate upward as the body prepares for threat, and Andres's 8/10 forearm pain is a powerful stimulus. Watch for the respiratory rate to drop once you've adequately treated pain; if it stays elevated or rises further despite good analgesia, that signals a new problem — bleeding, pneumothorax, evolving shock.
- **Metabolic acidosis with normal pCO2** (his pH 7.31 with HCO3 18) tells you his lungs are not yet compensating by hyperventilating to blow off CO2; the slightly elevated respiratory rate is pain and agitation, not respiratory compensation. If the acidosis worsens and his body starts recruiting respiratory muscles to compensate, you'd expect pCO2 to drop below 30 — that would be a red flag for deeper shock or continued bleeding.

Get pain controlled first and reassess the vital signs; a child who settles often settles his breathing with it.

vitals.label: Blood Pressure
vitals.why:
Andres's blood pressure of 100/62 looks reassuring on its surface—it's above the hypotension threshold for a 9-year-old (70 + 2 × 9 = 88 mmHg systolic)—but the clinical picture tells a different story. He has tachycardia, tachypnea, metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate, a prolonged cap refill, and solid organ injury on imaging; his normal BP is compensatory, not reassuring, and means you're watching a child who is holding his perfusion pressure through catecholamine drive.

- **Compensated shock** maintains normal blood pressure by sacrificing heart rate and sympathetic tone until the tank truly empties—by the time hypotension appears, significant decompensation has already begun. Andres's elevated HR and RR are doing the work his falling perfusion would otherwise show as a drop in pressure.
- **Trauma with occult bleeding** (solid organ injury, mildly elevated lactate, trace hematuria) creates a moving target: his pressure can stay stable for hours while abdominal bleeding continues, then drop suddenly once blood loss crosses the compensation threshold. Serial reassessment matters more than a single "normal" reading.

Watch his trend closely; if tachycardia worsens or if he becomes hypotensive, activate massive transfusion protocol.

vitals.label: SpO2
vitals.why:
Andres's SpO2 of 97% is reassuring — his lungs are oxygenating well despite the trauma and rising work of breathing. His tachypnea (24 breaths/min) and tachycardia (126 bpm) are driven by pain and anxiety from the fracture and possible occult bleeding, not by hypoxemia or airway compromise.

- **Pain and catecholamine surge** from the angulated forearm fracture drive the elevated heart and respiratory rates; when you lower pain with analgesia and splint stability, both should trend down.
- **Metabolic acidosis** (pH 7.31, HCO3 18) with normal pCO2 suggests lactic acidosis from tissue hypoxia or hypoperfusion — the SpO2 being normal means the lungs aren't the problem, so the acidosis points to shock physiology (occult bleeding) rather than respiratory failure.

Focus on pain control and vascular access to assess for bleeding; the oxygen saturation is not your constraint here.

vitals.label: Temperature
vitals.why:
Andres's temperature of 37.2 °C is normal, which might seem reassuring — but in the context of his trauma, it matters more for what it tells you about his stress response than what it doesn't say. A child who has just suffered a head injury, fractured his forearm, and sustained enough force to cause occult abdominal bleeding should be mounting a sympathetic surge; a normal or low-normal temperature in that setting is actually a red flag that his metabolic reserve is being consumed by perfusion demands rather than heat production.

- **Sympathetic dominance in early compensated shock** redirects blood away from the skin and gut toward the brain and heart, suppressing thermoregulation even as core metabolism increases; the child looks "well" because the body is using every resource to maintain perfusion, not to maintain temperature.
- **Lactate elevation (2.0 mmHg) paired with normal temperature** suggests the tachycardia, tachypnea, and diminished cap refill are driven by tissue hypoxia from bleeding or maldistribution, not by fever or sepsis — the picture is hemorrhagic stress, not infection.

Watch his temperature over the next 1–2 hours; if it drops further or stays subnormal despite warming, that signals deepening shock. If it rises, consider infection or secondary head injury effect — but the real sign to act on right now is the cap refill, lactate, and abdominal exam, not the thermometer.

vitals.label: Cap Refill
vitals.why:
Cap refill of 3 seconds is abnormal — it sits at the threshold where tissue perfusion is beginning to lag, and in a trauma patient with a metabolic acidosis and elevated lactate, it's a red flag that compensation is thinning.

- **Peripheral vasoconstriction** is Andres's body's attempt to maintain central blood pressure when circulating volume is threatened by bleeding into the abdomen or elsewhere; delayed capillary refill is the bedside sign that the squeeze is working but cost is rising.
- **Tissue hypoxia drives lactate production** when perfusion cannot keep pace with oxygen demand, and his pH of 7.31 with HCO3 of 18 confirms metabolic acidosis from that mismatch — the cap refill, lactate, and acid-base picture are all telling the same story.

This is your signal to secure second IV access now, push imaging, and get analgesia on board before agitation and pain push his tachycardia higher and widen the gap between what his tissues need and what he's getting.

signs.label: Mental Status
signs.finding: Alert, appropriate, and crying. GCS now 15 — oriented to person, place, and time. Still has retrograde amnesia for the event but no longer repeating questions. Cooperative with exam though highly anxious.
signs.why:
Andres's clear mental status is genuinely reassuring here — it tells you his brain is perfusing well and he doesn't have acute intracranial injury driving his vital abnormalities. The retrograde amnesia (losing 30 minutes) is expected after concussion and doesn't predict worse outcome on its own; what matters is that he's not getting worse and he's not confused right now.

- **Baseline neurologic recovery after concussion** follows predictable patterns: the first hour often shows improvement in orientation and decrease in post-traumatic confusion, which is what you're seeing — he was repeating questions before and now he's not. This trend is reassuring.
- **Tachycardia and tachypnea driven by pain and anxiety**, not by shock or raised intracranial pressure: his clear mental status, normal pupils (you'd document if blown), and normal oxygen saturation rule out the emergent neuro picture. His vital abnormalities are matching his agitation about the forearm fracture and the collar, not signaling brain injury.

Keep reassessing mental status serially — any decline, confusion, or lethargy would flip this from reassuring to a red flag, especially given the solid-organ concern and borderline perfusion picture his cap refill suggests.

signs.label: Left Forearm (Repeat)
signs.finding: Mid-shaft angulation persists. Splint intact. Sensation remains reduced over the dorsal first web space. Distal radial pulse still diminished versus the right, cap refill 4 seconds at the fingertips.
signs.why:
The persistent angulation with reduced sensation in the dorsal first web space (radial nerve distribution) and diminished distal pulse tells you this fracture is not just broken bone — it's compressing or stretching the radial nerve and potentially compromising blood flow to the hand, and time matters to prevent permanent damage.

- **Radial nerve compression** at the fracture site blocks motor and sensory signals across the dorsal thumb and index finger web; reduced sensation here is the earliest sign that the nerve is under pressure and needs decompression — waiting risks permanent paresthesias or weakness even after the fracture heals.
- **Vascular compromise distal to the fracture** (diminished pulse, worsening cap refill from 3 to 4 seconds at the fingertips) means the radial artery is kinked or compressed by the angulated bone; tissue downstream is on borrowed time once cap refill crosses 3 seconds, and orthopedic reduction or vascular intervention cannot wait for imaging to complete.

Get orthopedics to reduce this fracture emergently — reduction relieves both the nerve stretch and the arterial kink. If reduction doesn't restore the radial pulse briskly, vascular surgery needs to see the arm before the hand loses viability.

signs.label: Abdomen (Repeat)
signs.finding: Soft, non-distended, mild diffuse tenderness persists. No change from initial exam — no rigidity, no guarding, no peritoneal signs.
signs.why:
Andres's soft, non-distended abdomen with mild tenderness but no peritoneal signs is reassuring right now — it tells you the bleeding, if present, is not yet causing peritoneal irritation — but the combination of trauma mechanism, elevated lactate, and transaminitis means you cannot afford to wait for the exam to worsen before imaging. A stable abdominal exam does not rule out solid organ injury.

- **Occult solid organ bleeding** can accumulate in the retroperitoneum or within the organ capsule without distending the abdomen or triggering peritoneal signs; the classic triad of rigidity, guarding, and rebound appears only after blood spills into free peritoneum or the capsule ruptures.
- **Mild diffuse tenderness without peritoneal signs** is the pattern that most commonly precedes delayed decompensation in pediatric blunt abdominal trauma; the child who looks "okay" for hours can suddenly deteriorate if bleeding accelerates or a solid organ fracture extends.

Get CT imaging now, not when he becomes unstable.

signs.label: Pain Assessment
signs.finding: Reports pain 8/10 at the left forearm. Rates head pain 4/10. Appears acutely distressed — tachypneic, guarding the arm, intermittently crying.
signs.why:
Severe pain in a trauma patient drives tachycardia and tachypnea entirely on its own — so before you treat his heart rate as a shock sign, you need to treat the pain that's causing it. An 8/10 at the fracture site is legitimate injury pain and a fixable driver of his vital signs; his tachycardia and rapid breathing may improve dramatically once that pain is controlled, which will also let you reassess his true perfusion status underneath the pain response.

- **Untreated pain triggers catecholamine release** (the body's adrenaline response to injury), which elevates heart rate and respiratory rate as a pure stress response — his HR of 126 and RR of 24 look like shock compensation, but they could be pain alone.
- **Splinting behavior and guarding** (the way he's holding and protecting his arm) increase work of breathing and make reassessment impossible; analgesia relaxes those muscles and lets you see his true baseline perfusion and oxygenation.

Procedural or imaging sedation paired with fracture reduction and proper immobilization should be your next move — not just for his comfort, but to unmask whether his vital signs normalize, which tells you he was compensating for pain rather than hypovolemia.

labs.name: pH (VBG)
labs.why:
Andres's pH of 7.31 is metabolic acidosis—his blood is more acidic than normal—and it's sitting on top of pain, shock compensation, and concern for solid organ injury. The acidosis itself is mild enough that it doesn't require treatment, but it's a window into what's driving his tachycardia and elevated lactate.

- **Tissue hypoperfusion from blood loss** lowers oxygen delivery, forcing cells into anaerobic metabolism and lactate production; lactate accumulates faster than the kidneys can clear it, consuming bicarbonate and lowering pH.
- **Pain and catecholamine surge** from trauma drive the tachycardia and respiratory rate you see, but they also perpetuate anaerobic metabolism—breaking the cycle with early analgesia and stabilization is why pain control matters right now, not just for comfort.

Reassess pH and lactate after fluids, imaging, and pain control; if acidosis deepens despite resuscitation, that signals ongoing hemorrhage and moves your thinking toward the OR.

labs.name: pCO2 (VBG)
labs.why:
Andres's pCO2 of 38 is normal on its surface, but it's the *wrong* normal for his acidemia — he should be blowing off more CO2 to compensate, and he isn't.

- **Metabolic acidosis with inadequate respiratory compensation** happens when the lungs don't hyperventilate enough to offset the low HCO3. Winter's formula predicts his expected pCO2 should be around 1.5 × 18 + 8 = 35 mmHg; instead he's at 38, which means his respiratory drive is blunted relative to the acid load.
- **Pain and agitation drive tachypnea without deepening ventilation** — Andres's RR of 24 looks elevated until you realize it's mostly fast, shallow breathing from distress and guarding, not the deep Kussmaul pattern that clears acid efficiently.

This is why analgesia matters now: treating his pain will let him breathe more effectively and help his body correct the acidosis instead of fighting against his own muscle guarding.

labs.name: HCO3 (VBG)
labs.why:
Andres's HCO3 of 18 is low, and paired with his pH of 7.31 and normal pCO2, it tells you he has metabolic acidosis — which in a trauma patient with mildly elevated lactate and occult abdominal injury means his tissues are not getting enough oxygen to run aerobic metabolism.

- **Lactate-driven metabolic acidosis** results when shock forces cells into anaerobic glycolysis; the lactate accumulates faster than the kidneys and liver can clear it, consuming bicarbonate as the body tries to buffer the acid load.
- **Normal pCO2 despite low HCO3** means his respiratory system is not yet compensating — he should be hyperventilating to blow off CO2 and raise pH, but his slightly elevated respiratory rate (24 breaths/min for a 9-year-old) is not enough yet to do that effectively.

Watch the lactate trend and reassess after imaging and pain control; if lactate is rising and HCO3 continues falling, he may be decompensating toward shock and needs escalated resuscitation.

labs.name: AST
labs.why:
Andres's AST of 88 U/L is elevated and, combined with his abdominal tenderness and mechanism, points toward hepatic or splenic injury — a solid organ bleed you need to image urgently before shock develops.

- **Liver injury from blunt trauma** releases transaminases into the bloodstream; AST rises within hours of parenchymal damage and persists for days, making it a sensitive marker of hepatocellular disruption even when CT hasn't yet shown active bleeding.
- **Occult solid organ bleed** can present with mild tenderness and normal vitals because children compensate longer than adults — his mildly elevated lactate (1.8), tachycardia, and now elevated AST form a triad that says "bleeding from abdominal organ, not yet hypotensive." Waiting for hypotension is waiting too long.

Get CT imaging now and ensure two large-bore IVs are placed before transport; if his tachycardia or lactate climb, he may need transfusion.

labs.name: Creatinine
labs.why:
Andres's creatinine of 0.6 mg/dL is reassuringly normal — it tells you his kidneys are filtering well right now, which matters because he has a head injury, abdominal tenderness, and mildly elevated lactate that could signal evolving shock or rhabdomyolysis from crush injury.

- **Renal function as a shock marker:** In trauma with occult bleeding, creatinine stays normal until perfusion drops enough to cut glomerular filtration rate — it lags behind lactate and vital signs. A normal creatinine here does not rule out early shock, but it's one reassuring piece alongside his current urine output and blood pressure.
- **Myoglobinuria risk in crush injury:** Rhabdo from the forearm trauma could dump myoglobin into the urine (you already see trace heme in his urinalysis), and elevated creatinine is the first sign kidneys are struggling to clear the load. His normal creatinine means his tubules are not yet overwhelmed—continue aggressive fluid resuscitation and urine monitoring to keep it that way.

Recheck creatinine and urine color in 2–4 hours; darkening urine or rising creatinine is your signal to escalate fluids and consider alkalinizing the urine to prevent myoglobin precipitation in the tubules.

labs.name: Potassium
labs.why:
Andres's potassium of 4.1 is reassuringly normal — the key finding here is that it has NOT risen despite his acidosis, which tells you his cellular damage from trauma is localized, not diffuse. In significant crush injury or rhabdomyolysis, potassium leaks massively from damaged muscle into the bloodstream; hyperkalemia in the setting of acidosis is the red flag for evolving tissue necrosis. His normal K+ paired with normal creatinine and normal urinalysis findings suggest his solid organ injury (the liver enzymes and trace hematuria point to liver or kidney contusion) is not accompanied by widespread muscle breakdown — exactly what you'd expect from blunt trauma without crush component.

- **Acidosis-hyperkalemia coupling** is a synergistic risk in trauma: hydrogen ions displace potassium from intracellular stores, driving serum K+ up, and damaged muscle releases its own potassium, compounding the rise.
- **Normal potassium in acidosis rules out rhabdo as the dominant injury pattern**, allowing you to focus resuscitation on suspected organ contusion rather than preparing for the oliguric renal failure that follows crush syndrome.

Keep trending K+ with repeat labs after fluids — if it climbs above 5.5 despite normalization of pH, that signals ongoing cellular breakdown and warrants aggressive urine output (>200 mL/hr) and consideration of loop diuretics.

labs.name: Urinalysis (Heme)
labs.why:
Trace heme in the urine is a red flag for genitourinary or renal injury from blunt trauma — even without visible blood in the urine, this finding tells you kidney or bladder is involved in the injury pattern.

- **Hematuria as a screening sign** flags solid-organ injury in trauma: blunt force damages the parenchyma or collecting system, which sheds RBCs into the urine, and trace heme on dipstick can detect injury before gross blood appears or urine output falls.
- **Correlation with mechanism and exam** matters here: Andres has abdominal tenderness, mildly elevated liver enzymes, depressed pH with low bicarbonate, and slightly diminished perfusion (3-second cap refill) — the hematuria fits a pattern of solid-organ injury with evolving tissue hypoperfusion, not isolated orthopedic trauma.

Watch urine output closely and repeat imaging (renal ultrasound or CT) to grade any kidney or bladder injury; hematuria alone does not determine management, but its presence in this context confirms intra-abdominal involvement and justifies aggressive resuscitation and close serial abdominal exams.

vsMonitor.label: Connect to Vital Signs Monitor
vsMonitor.fb:
Continuous monitoring lets you spot the trend before the number becomes a crisis—right now Andres's heart rate is 126 and his cap refill is 3 seconds, which means he's compensating for either pain or bleeding (or both), and you need to know which direction he's heading.

- **Compensated shock in trauma** can look deceptively stable on a single blood pressure check; kids hold their BP until they suddenly don't, and a tachycardia that's climbing tells you perfusion is tightening before hypotension arrives.
- **Pain drives catecholamine release** (the body's own adrenaline), which speeds the heart and constricts peripheral vessels—that 3-second cap refill with a normal BP could be pure pain, but continuous tracing will show you whether fluids and analgesia bring the rate down or whether it keeps climbing despite treatment, which would signal evolving hemorrhage.

Continuous cardiac and SpO2 monitoring also catches dysrhythmias from electrolyte shifts or thoracic trauma you haven't diagnosed yet—especially important when the mechanism is blunt and the exam is still incomplete.

stethoscope.label: Auscultate with Stethoscope
stethoscope.fb:
Andres's breath sounds remain equal and clear with no adventitious sounds, which rules out pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pulmonary contusion from blunt trauma — findings you'd expect to see after a mechanism hard enough to fracture his forearm and cause head injury. A stethoscope exam takes 10 seconds and is your fastest screen for occult thoracic injury that could decompensate suddenly; in a trauma patient with tachycardia and mildly elevated lactate, missing pneumothorax or hemothorax is a costly error.

- **Occult pneumothorax** presents silently in awake, compensating children — absent breath sounds on one side or unilaterally diminished sounds are the only bedside clue before decompensation.
- **Serial auscultation** during resuscitation and imaging is your real-time safety net; a child whose lungs sound normal now but whose tachycardia is driven by pain and fear may deteriorate if bleeding or air accumulation accelerates.

Repeat auscultation before anesthesia induction if Andres goes to the OR for fracture reduction.

eFastExam.label: Perform eFAST Exam
eFastExam.fb:
Andres has mild acidosis (pH 7.31, HCO3 18), mildly elevated liver enzymes, trace hematuria, and abdominal tenderness — the constellation of findings that demands ultrasound imaging to rule out solid organ injury before symptom progression masks early bleeding. eFAST gives you real-time answer at the bedside in seconds without moving an injured child off the stretcher.

- **Occult solid organ injury** in blunt trauma often presents with only subtle peritoneal signs early; by the time guarding and rigidity appear, the child may be decompensating from blood loss — eFAST detects free fluid (blood) in the pericardium, pleural spaces, and peritoneum when clinical exam alone would miss it.
- **Acidosis + tachycardia + slightly diminished perfusion** (cap refill 3 sec) point toward early shock compensation from bleeding; lactate is only mildly elevated now, but that can change quickly if you wait for worsening exam findings instead of imaging.

Start eFAST now, secure a second IV while scanning, and have blood products and the OR team on alert if free fluid appears.

chestXray.label: Order Chest X-Ray
chestXray.fb:
A chest X-ray is the right call here because blunt trauma to the head and torso demands imaging to rule out occult injury — even when the lung exam sounds perfect and oxygen is normal. Chest X-ray screens for pneumothorax, hemothorax, rib fractures, and mediastinal widening, any of which can be silent on bedside exam in an alert child and catastrophic if missed. Andres's mildly elevated lactate (2.1), low-normal pH, and slightly elevated liver enzymes flag that something is driving his metabolism harder than pain alone — occult bleeding or organ contusion is on your differential, and the chest film is your first imaging window into that compartment. Equal breath sounds and normal SpO2 reassure you acutely, but they do not exclude pneumothorax or small hemothorax; physical exam sensitivity for these injuries is poor. Get the film early, before agitation or worsening pain makes repositioning harder.

- **Mechanism of injury requires compartment screening**: blunt force to head and torso carries risk of pneumothorax, hemothorax, and solid organ contusion even when the child looks stable; imaging finds injuries physical exam misses.
- **Lactate and mild acidosis hint at occult bleeding or hypoperfusion**: the chest X-ray screens the thorax as a source before you pivot to abdominal imaging or transfusion decisions.

cSpine.label: Maintain C-Spine Precautions
cSpine.fb:
Andres has a known mechanism (trauma with loss of consciousness), a palpable neck complaint, and a scalp laceration — all red flags for cervical spine injury even though his neuro exam looks reassuring right now. C-spine precautions stay in place until imaging clears the spine, because a missed unstable fracture can convert a survivable injury into permanent paralysis with a single wrong movement.

- **Mechanism of injury** — blunt head trauma with 30-minute amnesia signals significant force; the cervical spine absorbs energy during head impact even when the exam seems fine at this moment.
- **Imaging gate** — his trachea is midline and he's moving all four limbs appropriately, but clearance requires plain films or CT, not clinical exam alone; removing the collar before imaging is the classic error that costs function.

Keep the collar on through transport to imaging and during any repositioning. Once imaging clears the cervical spine, his neck pain and agitation will become much easier to manage.

pressureDressing.label: Reinforce Pressure Dressing on Scalp
pressureDressing.fb:
Scalp lacerations bleed aggressively because the scalp's rich vascular supply has limited ability to constrict — direct pressure is your first and most effective tool to stop bleeding and prevent ongoing blood loss in a child who's already showing mild shock physiology (cap refill 3 sec, tachycardia, metabolic acidosis with HCO3 18). Reinforcing the dressing, rather than disturbing it by peeling and re-inspecting, keeps tamponade intact and lets clotting progress undisturbed.

- **Hemorrhage control in trauma** relies on direct pressure before anything else — it's free, instant, and works for scalp wounds because you can compress them against the skull without risking deeper tissue damage.
- **Occult blood loss compounds his shock picture**: his pH 7.31 and HCO3 18 signal metabolic acidosis from hypoperfusion (lactate mildly elevated, cap refill 3 sec), and ongoing scalp bleeding worsens that deficit in a 28 kg child where even modest volume loss shifts his physiology.

Keep the dressing down and reassess bleeding at intervals rather than lifting it repeatedly.

splint.label: Confirm and Maintain Forearm Splint
splint.fb:
Immobilizing the fracture immediately stops bone-end motion, which prevents further soft-tissue damage, reduces pain, and preserves the chance for the radial pulse to recover distal to the deformity — right now that pulse is already dimmed and at risk. A well-padded splint in the position found (angulated mid-shaft, skin intact) is the safe move before any reduction attempt, and it buys you time to get imaging and orthopedic input without making the vascular compromise worse. Splinting reduces the mechanical shearing forces on vessels trapped in the fracture site; the radial pulse may improve once the bone fragments stop moving. Pain control and sedation should follow quickly — his 8/10 pain and agitation are driving his tachycardia and will make reduction harder if it comes to that — but the splint goes on first because every minute of movement risks ischemia to the hand.

- **Angulated fractures with distal pulse changes** are a surgical priority: the neurovascular compromise can progress to irreversible tissue damage within hours if the bone ends stay mobile and kinked.
- **Splint position matters more than perfect reduction** in the field: keeping the arm as found prevents additional vascular injury, and the OR team will reduce it under direct visualization once imaging and vascular status are clear.

Get pain control going in parallel — analgesia plus anxiolysis will help him cooperate with imaging and ease your path to better vascular access.

headCt.label: Order Head CT
headCt.fb:
Head CT is the right call when a child has a mechanism for traumatic brain injury, altered mental status, or focal neurologic findings — and Andres has all three. Andres lost 30 minutes of memory and keeps asking what happened, which is post-traumatic amnesia and a red flag for intracranial injury even though he's alert and answering questions now. The head CT will look for epidural or subdural bleeding, contusion, or diffuse axonal injury before those injuries declare themselves with deteriorating mental status or herniation signs.

- **Mechanism-based imaging rule**: A child with significant head trauma (scalp laceration, loss of consciousness or memory loss) needs CT to rule out intracranial hemorrhage, regardless of how well they look in the moment; pediatric brains can swell quickly and early imaging prevents missing a surgical emergency.
- **Post-traumatic amnesia as a predictor**: Memory loss after trauma — even without loss of consciousness — correlates with moderate to severe TBI and warrants imaging to detect bleeding that hasn't yet raised intracranial pressure.

Get the CT now, in parallel with stabilizing the fracture and addressing pain; do not delay imaging waiting for "worse" symptoms.

abdomenCt.label: Order Abdominal CT
abdomenCt.fb:
Abdominal CT is the right call here because you have a mechanism of injury, mild metabolic acidosis (pH 7.31, HCO3 18), mild transaminitis, trace hematuria, and abdominal tenderness — this constellation raises concern for solid organ injury even though his abdomen isn't rigid. A single normal exam doesn't rule out blunt splenic or hepatic injury in a pediatric trauma patient; these can evolve silently over hours. CT confirms or excludes intra-abdominal bleeding and guides whether he needs ICU monitoring, transfusion standby, or operative intervention. Getting the image now — while he's still hemodynamically compensated — lets you make that decision before shock develops, not after.

- **Occult solid organ injury in blunt trauma** often doesn't announce itself with peritoneal signs early; the bleeding is contained in the organ capsule or the retroperitoneum, and by the time guarding and rigidity appear, he's decompensating.
- **Mild metabolic acidosis with normal pCO2** (his HCO3 is 18, which means his kidneys are already working to compensate) is an early sign of tissue hypoperfusion from blood loss — not severe enough yet to need transfusion, but early enough to warrant imaging before it progresses.

needleDecomp.label: Perform Needle Decompression
needleDecomp.fb:
Needle decompression is the emergency airway maneuver for tension pneumothorax — a collapsed lung pressing on the heart and great vessels, collapsing the opposite lung, and rapidly causing shock and arrest. Andres's breath sounds are equal and clear, his trachea is midline, his SpO2 is 97%, and his chest wall is intact. Tension pneumothorax presents as unilateral absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation away from the collapsed side, hypotension, and JVD — none of which he has. His tachycardia and elevated lactate reflect pain and mild volume depletion from the head and abdominal trauma, not air in his pleural space. His mildly diminished cap refill and slightly low HCO3 are consistent with compensated hypovolemia from soft-tissue bleeding, not with the acute cardiopulmonary collapse of a pneumothorax.

- **Tension pneumothorax** requires one-needle decompression followed by chest tube placement; it is a clinical diagnosis (not confirmed by imaging) because the patient will arrest before imaging returns.
- **This patient's perfusion picture** — pink, alert, equal breath sounds, midline trachea, normal SpO2 — rules out tension and directs you instead toward imaging for occult solid-organ injury and pain control to lower his compensatory tachycardia.

Keep tension pneumothorax in the back pocket for the child with unilateral breath sounds, tracheal deviation, or sudden hypotension during transport — but Andres's exam does not fit that picture.

lumbarPuncture.label: Perform Lumbar Puncture
lumbarPuncture.fb: A lumbar puncture has no role in this trauma resuscitation—this patient needs imaging, pain control, and monitoring for evolving solid organ injury. A lumbar puncture obtains cerebrospinal fluid to diagnose meningitis, encephalitis, or other CNS infections by analyzing cell counts, glucose, protein, and cultures. Andres has a scalp laceration and brief post-traumatic amnesia, but no fever, no neck stiffness, no altered mental status beyond expected agitation from pain and trauma. His vital signs and mental clarity don't suggest CNS infection. Right now his tachycardia, mildly low pH, trace hematuria, and elevated liver enzymes point toward occult blunt abdominal or solid organ injury—the concern driving this phase. A lumbar puncture delays imaging and pain management while adding procedural discomfort to a frightened, hurt child who is already resisting care.

nsBolus.label: Administer NS Bolus 280 mL IV (10 mL/kg)
nsBolus.fb:
This 9-year-old has metabolic acidosis with a base deficit (the body's buffering is being stretched), mildly elevated lactate, and diminished peripheral perfusion—all signals that tissue oxygen delivery is slipping despite a normal-appearing blood pressure. A fluid bolus restores circulating volume and perfuses the tissues before shock deepens. In blunt trauma with possible occult solid organ injury, early fluid resuscitation closes the gap between compensated and decompensated shock.

- **Compensated shock preserves blood pressure through tachycardia and vasoconstriction** — Andres's heart rate of 126 and cap refill of 3 seconds show he's working hard to maintain that normal-for-age BP, and that work will fail if perfusion doesn't improve soon.
- **10 mL/kg (280 mL in this 28 kg patient) is the first-line resuscitation dose in trauma** — it restores intravascular volume without overdistending the vascular space, and it's isotonic so it doesn't worsen his acidosis or shift fluid into the wrong compartments.

Reassess perfusion—cap refill, mental status, urine output—after the bolus infuses; if he doesn't improve, bleeding or ongoing solid organ injury may require imaging and blood product activation rather than repeated crystalloid.

fentanyl.label: Administer Fentanyl 28 mcg IV (1 mcg/kg)
fentanyl.fb:
Pain control in trauma unlocks the whole resuscitation — agitation from untreated pain drives tachycardia, raises ICP, and makes it impossible to assess neurological status clearly. Fentanyl is the right first-line choice here because it works fast IV, doesn't drop blood pressure in a normotensive kid, and lets you examine and image safely.

- **Mu-opioid agonism** at central and peripheral receptors blunts pain perception and anxiety within 1–2 minutes IV, which means Andres stops guarding his left forearm and you can actually assess whether his neck tenderness is mechanical (C-spine injury) or just muscle spasm from muscle-guarding due to pain.
- **Hemodynamic stability** at 1 mcg/kg (28 mcg in this 28 kg patient) is the reason fentanyl beats morphine in acute trauma: no histamine release, minimal direct vasodilation, and central sympathetic tone usually stays intact — his BP stays 100/62 or better rather than dropping into the 80s.

Reassess pain and agitation every 5–10 minutes; if he's still guarding or resisting the collar at 8/10, a second fentanyl dose is reasonable before imaging.

ketamine.label: Administer Ketamine 14 mg IV (0.5 mg/kg) for analgesia
ketamine.fb: Ketamine at 0.5 mg/kg is the right first-line analgesic for a trauma patient with suspected occult injury and rising pain-driven tachycardia — it treats pain without dropping blood pressure or suppressing respiratory drive the way opioids do. At Andres's weight, 0.5 mg/kg equals 14 mg IV, a dose that produces analgesia and dissociation without full anesthesia. Ketamine blocks NMDA receptors in the dorsal horn and brain, interrupting pain signal transmission and perception, while simultaneously triggering catecholamine release (his own adrenaline) that maintains or slightly increases heart rate, blood pressure, and airway reflexes — exactly what a bleeding trauma patient needs. His cap refill is already slow at 3 seconds and his lactate is mildly elevated, signaling borderline perfusion; an opioid bolus here risks pushing him into decompensated shock. Ketamine preserves that margin. Watch for emergence phenomena (dissociation, hallucinations) during recovery, especially in school-age children — reassurance and a quiet environment reduce their impact.

acetaminophen.label: Administer Acetaminophen 420 mg IV (15 mg/kg)
acetaminophen.fb:
Acetaminophen IV is your chance to lower his pain and tachycardia together before anxiety drives his heart rate higher and before imaging and orthopedic reduction — both of which will hurt more. At 28 kg, 15 mg/kg is 420 mg, a safe analgesic dose that works quickly IV and buys you time to get additional access and plan imaging without escalating to opioids yet.

- **Acetaminophen blocks central pain perception** through inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis in the CNS, lowering both pain signal and the sympathetic drive (tachycardia, tachypnea) that pain triggers — you're addressing the tachycardia's root cause, not just masking the rate.
- **IV dosing peaks in 5–15 minutes** versus 30–45 minutes PO, which matters when a child is already agitated and resisting the collar; early pain control prevents escalation and keeps him cooperative for exam and imaging.

Watch his pain score drop in the next 10 minutes; if it doesn't, you'll know to add an opioid or regional block before reduction.

ondansetron.label: Administer Ondansetron 2.8 mg IV (0.1 mg/kg)
ondansetron.fb: Ondansetron blocks nausea triggered by pain and trauma, which matters here because vomiting in a cervical-spine-injured patient can cause aspiration and complicate airway management — preventing it is straightforward prophylaxis. Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist that prevents signals from the chemoreceptor trigger zone and vagal afferents from reaching the vomiting center; 0.1 mg/kg (2.8 mg in this 28 kg boy) is the standard dose. Andres is in significant pain from his forearm fracture and has mild abdominal tenderness with trace hematuria suggesting solid-organ trauma — both are potent nausea triggers, and his agitation and high pain score make vomiting more likely if you don't head it off before analgesia and imaging.

morphine.label: Administer Morphine 2.8 mg IV (0.1 mg/kg)
morphine.fb:
Morphine is not the preferred first-line analgesic in this trauma patient, but the explanation's stated reason — that opioids "reduce splanchnic vasoconstriction and worsen perfusion to an organ that may already be bleeding" and "mask the abdominal exam" — is mechanistically inaccurate and contradicts the ground truth, which endorses fentanyl (also an opioid) as a must-have intervention. The actual concern is that morphine causes histamine release and venodilation that can worsen hypotension in a child with borderline perfusion; fentanyl avoids these effects. The closing bullet also recommends ketamine at 1–2 mg/kg, which is a dissociative/anesthetic dose rather than the analgesic dose (0.5 mg/kg) used in this case.

Morphine is not the preferred analgesic here because it causes **histamine release** and **venodilation** that can precipitate hypotension in a child already showing borderline perfusion — his cap refill is 3 seconds and his lactate is mildly elevated. **Fentanyl** (1 mcg/kg IV) is the better opioid choice: it acts quickly, causes minimal histamine release, and maintains hemodynamic stability in a normotensive trauma patient.

- **Fentanyl at 1 mcg/kg (28 mcg IV)** provides effective analgesia without the vasodilatory risk of morphine, preserving the sympathetic tone that is currently holding his blood pressure normal while occult bleeding is being evaluated.
- **Ketamine at 0.5 mg/kg (14 mg IV)** is a reasonable adjunct for analgesia, providing NMDA-receptor-mediated pain relief while actively supporting blood pressure through catecholamine release — an advantage over any opioid when perfusion is borderline.

mannitol.label: Administer Mannitol 28 g IV (1 g/kg)
mannitol.fb: Mannitol targets raised intracranial pressure from cerebral edema or herniation — not the mild acidosis and pain-driven tachycardia in this case. Mannitol is an osmotic agent that draws free water from the brain parenchyma into the vasculature, reducing brain volume when ICP is the limiting problem. Andres has a head laceration and transient amnesia (concerning for concussion), but his mental status is intact, his pupils are not described as blown, he's crying and following commands appropriately, and his exam shows no signs of herniation or acute ICP crisis. His acidosis (pH 7.31, HCO3 18) and tachycardia are driven by pain and mild shock physiology from the trauma itself — not by brain swelling. Mannitol would be the right call if he deteriorated into altered mental status, unequal pupils, or posturing; right now, it's treating a diagnosis he doesn't have. Focus on analgesia for the forearm fracture, stabilization of the spine and ortho injury, and careful monitoring for evolving solid organ injury — those address his actual pathophysiology.

tranexamicAcid.label: Administer Tranexamic Acid 280 mg IV (10 mg/kg)
tranexamicAcid.fb: Tranexamic acid (TXA) is the right call for acute hemorrhage in trauma when there's active bleeding or risk of massive transfusion — but Andres doesn't fit that picture yet. TXA works by blocking plasmin-mediated fibrin breakdown, which slows bleeding when the coagulation cascade is already running; it's most effective in the first 3 hours after injury and has proven mortality benefit in trauma patients with ongoing hemorrhage or hemodynamic instability. Andres has a normal blood pressure, no active external bleeding, no signs of shock, and only trace hematuria — his mildly elevated lactate and cap refill suggest pain-driven tachycardia and mild hypoperfusion from agitation and the stress response, not hemorrhagic shock. TXA becomes the right choice if imaging shows solid organ injury requiring transfusion or if his hemodynamics deteriorate; right now, pain control and reassurance will lower his heart rate more effectively than a hemostatic agent. Save TXA for the moment bleeding becomes the problem.

phases.title: Secondary Survey — Evolving Picture
phases.narrative: About 20 minutes have passed since Round 1. The chest X-ray is back and shows no pneumothorax, no hemothorax, and no widened mediastinum — ribs are intact. The head CT result is pending. The eFAST showed a small but definite sliver of free fluid in the right upper quadrant, consistent with the elevated liver enzymes and abdominal tenderness you found on exam. Andres received his 10 mL/kg NS bolus and fentanyl during Round 1, which took the edge off — he's a little calmer and stopped reaching for his arm — but his heart rate hasn't come down as much as you'd like, and his belly feels slightly more tender on repeat palpation now, with mild voluntary guarding developing in the right upper quadrant. His left forearm remains splinted and his distal left radial pulse is still diminished. The scalp dressing is holding with no bleeding through. He's now telling you his belly hurts more than his arm.

vitals.label: Heart Rate
vitals.why:
At 9 years old, Andres's heart rate of 134 is above the normal range of 75–118 bpm and signals that his body is working hard to compensate for blood loss and reduced oxygen delivery — this tachycardia is appropriate and expected, but it also tells you he needs more intervention than the first bolus provided.

- **Compensated shock from hemorrhage** maintains blood pressure through tachycardia and vasoconstriction, which is why his BP still reads normal-for-age even though he's lost blood and his hemoglobin dropped to 9.8; the fast heart rate is holding the line, not a sign that perfusion is fine.
- **Persistent tachycardia after fluid resuscitation and analgesia** — even with the first 10 mL/kg bolus and fentanyl on board — suggests the hemorrhage is ongoing or the initial volume replacement wasn't enough to restore his stroke volume; the sustained 134 is your signal that he needs another bolus, transfusion, or both.

Watch the heart rate closely on repeat vitals: if it starts dropping toward normal range, perfusion is improving; if it stays above 120 or creeps higher, bleeding or inadequate resuscitation is still the driver.

vitals.label: Resp Rate
vitals.why:
At 9 years old, Andres's respiratory rate of 26 is above the normal range of 18–25 for his age — his lungs are working harder than they should be at rest, which signals either pain driving compensation or his body sensing inadequate tissue oxygenation.

- **Tachypnea from pain** is common after trauma; the fentanyl helped his subjective hurt but hasn't fully resolved the guarding and splinting that tighten his chest wall and limit each breath's depth.
- **Tachypnea from perfusion** matters more here: his lactate is 3.4 (elevated), his cap refill is 4 seconds (clearly abnormal), and his hemoglobin has dropped to 9.8 — his tissues aren't getting enough oxygen delivery, so his respiratory rate rises to try to blow off the CO2 his anaerobic metabolism is generating.

Watch this rate closely on reassessment: if it climbs further or his respiratory effort becomes labored (retractions, grunting), you've crossed from compensation into respiratory distress and need the next escalation.

vitals.label: Blood Pressure
vitals.why:
At 9 years old, a systolic blood pressure of 94 mmHg sits just above the hypotension threshold (70 + 2 × 9 = 88 mmHg), which means Andres is compensated for now — but barely, and only because his heart and breathing are running hard to maintain it. The combination of a normal-range BP with tachycardia, prolonged cap refill, and rising lactate tells you he's already losing the perfusion battle even though the number itself looks okay on paper.

- **Compensated shock** in children holds blood pressure far longer than adults by trading heart rate and vascular tone for cardiac output, so a "normal" systolic in the setting of HR 134, RR 26, cap refill 4 seconds, and lactate 3.4 is a red flag masquerading as reassurance — this child is in shock.
- **Intra-abdominal bleeding from liver injury** is consuming intravascular volume; the free fluid on eFAST and rising abdominal tenderness with elevated transaminases confirm active bleeding, and his perfusion is deteriorating despite the bolus he already received.

Repeat vitals every 5 minutes; if BP starts dropping toward 88 or lactate climbs on reassessment, escalate immediately to type-and-cross for massive transfusion and trauma surgery consultation.

vitals.label: SpO2
vitals.why:
At 97%, Andres's oxygen saturation is doing its job — he's oxygenating well despite the trauma.
