The reason to note it here is what it tells you he is NOT: he's not in respiratory distress from a pneumothorax or hemothorax (chest X-ray confirmed both are absent), and his airway is patent and unobstructed. In a 9-year-old with blunt head and truncal trauma, a normal SpO2 rules out a major immediately life-threatening chest injury and lets you focus on the bleeding you can see — the liver laceration driving his rising abdominal tenderness and persistent tachycardia.

- **Oxygenation reserve in pediatrics** means children can maintain normal SpO2 even while compensating heavily with tachycardia and tachypnea for blood loss; normal SpO2 does not mean normal perfusion, and his heart rate of 134 and rising belly pain tell you perfusion is stressed.
- **Reassuring vital in isolation can mask decompensation** — his SpO2 staying normal while his cap refill lengthens to 4 seconds and his lactate rises to 3.4 mmol/L means the problem is hemorrhagic shock, not respiratory failure, and requires blood products and surgical evaluation, not more oxygen.

Watch for SpO2 to drop only after his circulating volume falls further — by then he'll need type-and-cross and the OR, not just fluids.

vitals.label: Temperature
vitals.why:
Andres's temperature of 37.3 °C is normal and reassuring, which matters because it tells you his core physiology is not yet fighting a systemic inflammatory response to his injuries — but it also means the tachycardia and elevated lactate you're seeing are driven purely by hypovolemia and pain, not by fever masking additional sepsis or head injury complications.

- **Hemorrhagic shock in children maintains normothermia early** because the body's heat-generating mechanisms (shivering, peripheral vasoconstriction) are overridden by the need to dump heat from compensatory tachycardia and muscle tension; hypothermia appears later as shock deepens and perfusion fails.
- **Absent fever with blunt head trauma** is reassuring for uncomplicated concussion or minor intracranial injury; if the head CT returns abnormal with intracranial bleeding or swelling, fever would typically emerge over hours as inflammation develops, so a normal temperature now leaves that window still open but does not guarantee absence of injury.

Watch the temperature trend: any rise over the next 2–4 hours signals inflammatory cascade or evolving infection from translocation if abdominal injury worsens.

vitals.label: Cap Refill
vitals.why:
A capillary refill of 4 seconds is clearly abnormal and signals that Andres's tissues are not receiving enough blood flow — this is the earliest bedside clue that his bleeding is catching up with his compensation.

- **Prolonged capillary refill reflects peripheral vasoconstriction** driven by his body's attempt to redirect blood toward the core (heart, brain, liver) when total circulating volume is shrinking; his skin beds are sacrificed to preserve vital organs.
- **The mismatch between normal blood pressure and slow cap refill is the danger sign here**: his BP of 94/58 is still above the hypotension threshold for a 9-year-old, but the slow cap refill + tachycardia + rising lactate + worsening abdominal tenderness tell you he's already in compensated shock and bleeding into his abdomen — the BP will drop soon if you don't intervene.

Repeat the cap refill every few minutes and watch for it to worsen or his BP to drop; either one means move to the next level of resuscitation (type and cross for transfusion, consider vasopressor support if pressors become necessary).

signs.label: Mental Status
signs.finding: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. GCS 15. Anxious and increasingly distressed, pointing to his right upper quadrant. No longer asking repetitive questions.
signs.why:
Andres's clear orientation and GCS of 15 is reassuring — his head CT is still pending, but his brain is perfusing and functioning right now. The shift from repetitive questions about "what happened" to focused complaint about his belly pain is actually important: he's stopped the acute confusion of head trauma and is now localizing to the real problem driving his physiology.

- **Posttraumatic amnesia** typically resolves over minutes to hours in mild-to-moderate head injury; the fact that he's tracking time and people now, even while anxious, means his reticular activating system is intact and intracranial pressure is not yet threatening his level of consciousness.
- **Pain-driven anxiety and tachycardia** explain his current distress better than shock does — his GCS is perfect, his skin is still perfusing (cap refill is concerning but not yet suggesting altered mental status from hypoperfusion), and his complaint is anatomically specific to the liver injury you're already treating.

Watch the head CT when it returns; if it shows significant injury, his mental status can deteriorate fast as edema develops. For now, his clear sensorium tells you his bleeding and shock picture is not yet severe enough to compromise brain perfusion.

signs.label: Abdomen
signs.finding: Mild voluntary guarding now present in the right upper quadrant. Tenderness on palpation is more focal and more intense than the initial exam — right upper quadrant worse than diffuse. No rebound tenderness elicited. Abdomen remains non-distended.
signs.why:
Worsening abdominal tenderness with new focal guarding in the right upper quadrant tells you bleeding is active — the eFAST showed free fluid there, and Andres's belly is becoming more tender, not less, despite pain control and fluids. This is the pattern of ongoing hemorrhage, not just bruising from impact.

- **Voluntary guarding** (the patient tightens his muscles to protect a sore spot) signals peritoneal irritation from blood accumulation rather than deep organ injury alone; it develops over minutes to hours as blood pools, which is exactly what you're seeing now.
- **Progressive tenderness despite analgesia and resuscitation** is the red flag — a child who got pain control and fluids should feel better if bleeding has stopped, not worse. Andres is telling you with his belly that the bleeding is continuing.

Watch for rebound tenderness (pain on release, worse than on press) and abdominal distension — either one means decompensating hemorrhagic shock. This child needs the OR.

signs.label: Skin / Perfusion
signs.finding: Skin still warm centrally but extremities are cooler than on arrival. Mild pallor has worsened slightly. No new bruising or ecchymosis.
signs.why:
Andres's cooling extremities and worsening pallor are the first visible signs that his body is redirecting blood away from the skin toward his vital organs — a compensatory response to blood loss that means shock is tightening its grip. His blood pressure is still in the normal-for-age range, which is why it's easy to miss, but capillary refill of 4 seconds and diminished radial pulse at his injury site confirm perfusion is under real strain.

- **Catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction** pulls blood from the skin and splanchnic bed toward the heart and brain; the cool extremities and pallor you see are the physical proof that his sympathetic nervous system is working hard to maintain central pressure as his circulating volume drops from the liver bleed.
- **Progressive compensation** means the next phase is decompensation — once the body can no longer hold blood pressure by squeezing peripheral vessels, hypotension arrives suddenly and catastrophically, making this the moment to act before the crisis deepens.

This is the time for aggressive resuscitation: repeat fluid bolus, activate massive transfusion protocol with pRBC and FFP, and prepare for OR evaluation of the liver injury.

signs.label: Left Forearm
signs.finding: Angulated deformity persists. Splint intact and in good position. Sensation remains reduced over the dorsal first web space. Distal radial pulse is still diminished but present.
signs.why:
The diminished radial pulse distal to the angulation is a vascular red flag that demands immediate reduction—this fracture is compressing the radial artery and risking hand ischemia if left uncorrected. Reduced sensation in the first web space (radial nerve territory) confirms nerve compromise alongside the vascular issue, narrowing the window to restore perfusion before tissue damage becomes irreversible.

- **Vascular compromise in fractures** occurs when bone edges or swelling compress adjacent arteries; the longer the compression persists, the greater the risk of thrombosis, distal tissue necrosis, and permanent loss of function in the hand.
- **Nerve injury patterns** in mid-shaft radius fractures classically involve radial nerve stretching or compression, producing loss of sensation in the dorsal first web space—exactly what you're seeing—and motor weakness in wrist/thumb extension; persistent compression compounds both.

Splint reduction attempts in the ED are reasonable here given the vascular and neurologic signs, with orthopedic standby; if reduction doesn't restore the pulse within minutes, prepare for operative reduction in the OR.

signs.label: Breath Sounds
signs.finding: Equal and clear bilaterally. No adventitious sounds. Trachea midline. No signs of developing pneumothorax.
signs.why:
Equal and clear breath sounds with a midline trachea are reassuring because they tell you the chest trauma — despite the force of impact — has not torn lung or pleura or shifted the mediastinum. In blunt thoracic trauma, a pneumothorax or hemothorax would narrow your resuscitation options and demand immediate decompression or chest tube placement; their absence buys you time to focus on the intra-abdominal bleeding that is actually driving Andres's shock picture.

- **Thoracic integrity** means his hypoxemia risk is low and his shock is hemorrhagic (from the liver laceration), not compressive—you can treat it with fluid and blood products rather than an emergency needle decompression.
- **Midline trachea** rules out tension physiology, which would cause hemodynamic collapse and altered mental status; Andres remains awake and oriented, and his airway is uncompromised.

Keep reassessing the lungs every few minutes as fluid resuscitation continues — massive transfusion and positive-pressure ventilation can unmask a small pneumothorax that was sealed by low intrathoracic pressure at arrival.

signs.label: Scalp Laceration
signs.finding: Pressure dressing intact and dry. No bleed-through. No new neurological complaints; no worsening headache reported.
signs.why:
The scalp laceration is a visible entry wound from the impact, but the fact that the dressing is holding dry and he has no new neurological complaints tells you the primary injury is not the laceration itself — it's the underlying head trauma. A scalp wound can bleed briskly because the scalp is highly vascular, but pressure controls it reliably; what matters now is whether the blow caused intracranial injury. His appropriate mental status and stable neuro exam are reassuring, but the head CT that's pending will show whether there's a concussion, contusion, or — less likely at his level of alertness — intracranial bleeding. Keep the dressing in place, watch for any change in behavior, drowsiness, or new headache, and once the CT clears him, the laceration itself will need cleaning and closure, but that's a lower priority than ruling out the head injury underneath.

- **Scalp wounds bleed heavily because the scalp's blood vessels don't retract when cut** — pressure dressing works well because it's direct compression of the bleeding source, not treatment of the trauma itself.
- **The real injury is the acceleration-deceleration force transmitted to the brain tissue**, which may cause bruising, swelling, or bleeding inside the skull even when the scalp wound looks minor.

Watch for lethargy, vomiting, or irritability over the next 24 hours — those would be signs of evolving intracranial pressure.

signs.label: Pain Assessment
signs.finding: Reports abdominal pain now 7/10, worse than his arm pain which has improved to 4/10 after fentanyl. Appears visibly uncomfortable and is splinting his breathing with deep inspiration.
signs.why:
Andres's escalating abdominal pain despite analgesia is a red flag for evolving intra-abdominal injury — the eFAST already showed free fluid in the right upper quadrant, and pain that worsens after initial resuscitation signals ongoing bleeding or organ damage, not just contusion settling.

- **Pain out of proportion to exam** is the classic teaching point in blunt trauma, but the flip side matters here: pain that gets worse after fluids and analgesia, while the exam becomes more tender, tells you the bleeding is active and not slowing down. His hemoglobin is 9.8 and his lactate is 3.4 — both consistent with blood loss — and now the pain is shouting the same message his labs are whispering.
- **Splinting on deep inspiration** means his abdominal wall muscles are bracing to protect the injured liver or spleen from movement. Watch for this to deepen — worsening splinting with shallow breathing can signal peritoneal irritation and a slide toward decompensation.

Escalate to the trauma team and surgeon now; this child needs operative evaluation and possibly the OR.

labs.name: Hemoglobin
labs.why:
Andres's hemoglobin of 9.8 is low because he's bleeding into his abdomen — the eFAST already showed free fluid in the right upper quadrant, and his liver enzymes are elevated, meaning blunt force trauma to the liver is the culprit. This is not anemia from poor nutrition or chronic disease; this is acute blood loss, and the number tells you how much he's already lost.

- **Acute hemorrhage dilutes the hemoglobin concentration** as the body shifts interstitial fluid into the vascular space to restore volume — so the hemoglobin falls faster than the actual red cell mass does, and a single low number underestimates total blood loss.
- **Lactate of 3.4 paired with a low hemoglobin signals tissue hypoperfusion from bleeding**, not infection or primary shock — his lactate is climbing because oxygen delivery to tissues is dropping as his red cell count falls and his heart has to work harder (HR 134, cap refill 4 seconds) to push what cells remain around the circuit.

Watch the hemoglobin trend on the next draw — if it's falling faster than fluids alone can explain, that's your signal the bleeding is continuing and he needs either a second bolus, blood product, or operative intervention.

labs.name: Hematocrit
labs.why:
At 9 years old, Andres's hematocrit of 29% is below the normal range for his age and signals blood loss from the blunt abdominal trauma — this is the hemoglobin and hematocrit pair telling you he's bleeding into his abdomen right now, not just bruised.

- **Acute hemorrhage lowers oxygen-carrying capacity.** The drop in hematocrit reflects real blood loss into the peritoneal cavity where it cannot deliver oxygen to tissues; paired with his elevated lactate of 3.4 and prolonged cap refill of 4 seconds, the picture is compensated hemorrhagic shock — his heart rate and respiratory rate are climbing to maintain delivery despite fewer red cells.
- **Liver injury bleeds slowly but persistently.** The elevated transaminases (ALT 118, AST 154) and the eFAST finding of free fluid in the right upper quadrant point to hepatic parenchymal damage; the liver is a highly vascular organ and even a minor laceration can produce ongoing slow bleeding that accumulates over minutes to hours.

Watch the hematocrit trend on repeat labs in 2–4 hours — if it's falling despite your fluid resuscitation, you're losing the race and the child needs operative hemostasis.

labs.name: Lactate
labs.why:
Andres's lactate of 3.4 is elevated because his tissues aren't getting enough oxygen relative to what they need — a sign that his shock is already present, even though his blood pressure still looks normal for his age. This is exactly why you can't trust the BP alone in a 9-year-old; kids maintain blood pressure by squeezing harder (tachycardia, vasoconstriction) until they suddenly can't, so lactate is your early warning that the tank is running dry.

- **Anaerobic metabolism** kicks in when oxygen delivery drops below what the cells demand, forcing them to make energy without oxygen and producing lactate as a byproduct — this happens in hemorrhagic shock before hypotension appears.
- **Tissue hypoperfusion** from blood loss (the abdominal free fluid and hemoglobin drop point to ongoing bleeding) shifts the balance between oxygen supply and cellular demand, raising lactate faster than compensatory tachycardia can restore balance.

A lactate this high on top of mild hypotension, persistent tachycardia despite analgesia, and worsening abdominal tenderness means the initial bolus bought time but not control — he needs imaging to define the bleeding source and likely needs blood products, not more crystalloid alone.

labs.name: ALT
labs.why:
Andres's elevated ALT signals hepatocellular injury from blunt trauma — the liver took a direct hit, and the enzyme rise confirms it. This matters because ALT rises fastest in acute injury and trails off over hours, so this number tells you the damage is fresh and active right now, not old.

- **Hepatocellular leak** means liver cells are breaking open and spilling their enzymes into the bloodstream; ALT is more liver-specific than AST, so a disproportionately high ALT points squarely at the liver rather than muscle or other organs.
- **Bleeding risk rises with liver injury** because the liver makes clotting factors — his INR is already slightly elevated at 1.3, and worsening transaminitis predicts worsening coagulopathy if bleeding continues.

Watch the repeat labs in 2–4 hours: a falling hemoglobin or rising lactate despite the IV bolus means he's still bleeding into the abdomen and needs the next level of resuscitation or imaging-guided intervention (imaging is pending for head; consider CT abdomen/pelvis next if the picture doesn't improve).

labs.name: AST
labs.why:
AST of 154 is high because the liver has been traumatized and is leaking hepatic enzymes into the bloodstream — it's direct evidence of the blunt abdominal injury you suspected from the free fluid on ultrasound and the rising abdominal tenderness. The degree of elevation (nearly 4× normal) correlates with severity of liver injury, though the exact enzyme level doesn't perfectly predict whether operative intervention will be needed.

- **Hepatocellular injury releases transaminases.** When the liver parenchyma is damaged by blunt force, AST and ALT spill into the blood; AST is slightly more liver-specific in the context of isolated hepatic trauma and tends to rise a bit higher than ALT during acute hepatic necrosis.
- **Lactate elevation adds concern for tissue hypoperfusion.** Your lactate of 3.4 paired with the high transaminases and the drop in hemoglobin tells you this child has bled into the abdominal cavity — the liver injury is not just cellular damage, it's a source of ongoing or recent hemorrhage that's consuming his circulating volume.

Watch the trend: if AST climbs further on recheck in 4–6 hours, escalate imaging (CT abdomen with contrast) and prepare for possible ICU/OR involvement.

labs.name: INR
labs.why:
An INR of 1.3 signals early coagulopathy — your first warning that Andres is losing the race between bleeding and clotting. In blunt abdominal trauma with liver injury, this modest elevation matters because it reflects consumption of clotting factors faster than the liver can replenish them, and it predicts a downslope if transfusion doesn't interrupt the cycle.

- **Consumptive coagulopathy** begins when liver laceration releases tissue factor into the bloodstream, triggering massive clot formation in and around the wound, which exhausts platelets and factors faster than the liver's synthetic capacity can match — the INR climbs as factors II, V, VII, and X become depleted.
- **Hepatic synthetic dysfunction** compounds the picture here: the elevated liver enzymes (AST 154, ALT 118) indicate hepatocyte damage from the blunt impact, and damaged hepatocytes produce clotting factors more slowly just when demand is highest, locking Andres into a vicious cycle of worsening coagulopathy.

Watch the INR trend closely — if it rises to >1.5 or the fibrinogen drops below 100 mg/dL, activation of massive transfusion protocol (1:1:1 pRBC:FFP:platelet ratio) becomes urgent, not optional.

labs.name: Creatinine
labs.why:
Andres's creatinine of 0.6 is reassuring right now, but it's masking the real story — he has active bleeding into his belly and his kidneys haven't yet felt the squeeze of losing blood volume. Creatinine rises only after glomerular filtration drops, which means a normal creatinine in early shock can be dangerously false reassurance.

- **Renal perfusion lags behind systemic perfusion.** His lactate of 3.4 and cap refill of 4 seconds show he's already maldistributing blood away from skin and gut; the kidneys compensate longer than other organs, so creatinine stays normal even as tissue hypoxia is building elsewhere.
- **Hemoglobin of 9.8 with ongoing abdominal tenderness means he's still bleeding.** Once he loses enough intravascular volume, renal perfusion will drop and creatinine will climb — but by then he'll need blood products, not just crystalloid, and may be approaching the point where fluids alone won't save him.

Watch the creatinine trend and the urine output closely on the next round; a rising creatinine or dropping urine output in the next 1–2 hours would signal progressive shock despite resuscitation and demand immediate escalation to the OR.

labs.name: Glucose
labs.why:
Andres's glucose of 112 is reassuringly normal, which matters because trauma and pain trigger a stress response that can push glucose sky-high — if his glucose were elevated despite adequate resuscitation, it would signal either a deeper physiologic insult or poor pain control.

- **Stress hyperglycemia** from catecholamine surge (adrenaline and cortisol released by trauma) typically raises glucose 150–250 mg/dL in children, especially in the first hours after injury; a normal value here means his endocrine response is tracking appropriately without exaggerated release.
- **Normal glucose with abnormal lactate** (3.4 mmol/L) and prolonged cap refill (4 sec) tells you the hypoperfusion is real — tissue hypoxia is driving anaerobic metabolism and lactate rise — but his pancreas is still responding normally to insulin, so you're not yet in the decompensated shock zone where glucose and lactate both run high and mental status deteriorates.

Keep tracking lactate on reassessment; if it rises while glucose stays normal, that's your signal the bleeding outpaces fluid resuscitation and he needs the next intervention — either more aggressive fluid dosing or blood product consideration.

labs.name: Potassium
labs.why:
Potassium of 4.3 is normal right now, but it's a deceptive reassurance in a bleeding trauma patient because the real total-body potassium is almost certainly depleted — you're just seeing a normal serum value while intracellular stores are being consumed.

- **Dilutional hypokalemia masks total-body deficit.** Andres received a 10 mL/kg NS bolus, which dilutes his serum potassium without replacing what his cells have lost from bleeding and tissue injury; a "normal" K+ in the setting of hemorrhage is often a marker that total-body stores are already low.
- **Metabolic acidosis from shock (lactate 3.4) would normally push potassium OUT of cells and raise serum K+.** The fact that his K+ is still in the lower half of normal despite ongoing hypoperfusion tells you his total-body potassium is severely depleted — once you give blood products and restore perfusion, serum K+ will drop further as acidosis corrects and potassium shifts back into cells.

Recheck K+ before any ongoing resuscitation; if it stays normal or creeps up as lactate falls, suspect ongoing hemorrhage. A potassium that crashes once you start correcting the acidosis is expected and demands aggressive replacement.

labs.name: Sodium
labs.why:
Andres's sodium of 136 is technically within the normal range, but paired with his trauma picture it deserves a second look — he's lost blood volume and received a bolus of normal saline, yet his sodium hasn't climbed. Sodium naturally rises during hemorrhagic shock as free water shifts out of cells and into the vascular space to compensate; a "normal" sodium in this context can mask ongoing volume loss.

- **Relative hyponatremia in hemorrhage** means the sodium hasn't concentrated the way you'd expect it to in a bleeding patient, suggesting his fluid losses may be outpacing his resuscitation — the bolus bought time but the bleeding hasn't stopped.
- **Saline tonicity** (0.9% NS is isotonic) neither concentrates nor dilutes serum sodium, so a repeat bolus or transition to blood products will be needed to restore the osmotic pull that keeps intracellular fluid where it belongs.

Watch the sodium trend on the next lab draw; if it drifts down while the lactate stays high, you're losing the race against ongoing hemorrhage.

phases.title: Hemorrhage Control and Surgical Escalation
phases.narrative: The picture is sharpening: Andres has a falling hemoglobin, rising lactate, and an eFAST with free fluid in the right upper quadrant. His liver enzymes are doubling and the RUQ tenderness is more focal now. His BP has slipped a bit despite the Round 1 fluid bolus, and his tachycardia has climbed. He's bleeding — likely from a hepatic laceration — and he's not compensating well enough on his own. The abdominal CT will characterize the injury, but while that's being arranged, this is the moment to shore up his intravascular volume, get surgery on the phone, and make sure you have the vascular access to keep up if he declares himself further. His airway remains his own, his mental status is intact, and the head CT is still pending — keep him in the collar and watch closely.

vitals.label: Heart Rate
vitals.why:
At 9 years old, Andres's heart rate of 138 bpm is high-normal to mildly elevated for his age (normal range 75–118 at rest), but what makes it clinically important right now is that it's climbing despite already having received one fluid bolus — that trajectory signals he's losing the race between bleeding and compensation. His heart is racing to maintain cardiac output as his circulating blood volume shrinks from the hepatic laceration, and the fact that his BP is still technically normal-for-age masks the real story: he's using up his compensatory reserve.

- **Decompensation in hemorrhagic shock unfolds in stages.** Early hemorrhage triggers catecholamine (adrenaline) release, which drives tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction to keep the brain and heart perfused; blood pressure stays near-normal because vasoconstriction compensates for lost volume. A rising heart rate despite fluid resuscitation means the bleeding is outpacing the fluid going in, and the next domino is hypotension.
- **Cap refill of 4 seconds paired with tachycardia of 138 tells you he's already in the compensated phase.** The prolonged refill reflects the peripheral vasoconstriction keeping his core perfused — that's what keeps his BP from dropping, but it also means his skin, extremities, and gut are being sacrificed to protect his vital organs. His elevated lactate (3.4) confirms tissue hypoperfusion is already driving anaerobic metabolism.

Recheck vitals every 5–10 minutes and prepare for rapid escalation: second large-bore IV or IO access, type & cross blood products, and surgical consultation should already be underway — if his BP drops or he becomes difficult to arouse, you are moving to the OR.

vitals.label: Resp Rate
vitals.why:
Andres's respiratory rate of 26 is above the normal range for a 9-year-old (18–25 br/min) and signals that his body is working hard to compensate for blood loss — tachypnea is an early warning sign of shock before blood pressure drops. His lungs are clear and his oxygen level is fine, so this fast breathing is not about hypoxemia; it's about metabolic acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion.

- **Anaerobic metabolism** occurs when oxygen delivery falls short of tissue demand, forcing cells to switch to inefficient pathways that produce lactate instead of CO2 — his lactate of 3.4 mmol/L confirms ongoing tissue hypoxia despite a normal-range blood pressure.
- **Respiratory compensation** for metabolic acidosis kicks in automatically: faster breathing blows off CO2 and raises serum pH toward normal, a reflex that keeps his acid-base balance from collapsing while you restore perfusion.

The tachypnea paired with his falling hemoglobin, elevated lactate, and diminishing perfusion (cap refill 4 seconds) means he is in compensated shock from bleeding and will decompensate without volume and surgical intervention soon.

vitals.label: Blood Pressure
vitals.why:
At 9 years old, Andres's blood pressure of 92/56 sits right at the threshold — technically normal-for-age by the 5th percentile rule, but already telling you he's working hard to stay there. His tachycardia of 138, capillary refill of 4 seconds, and rising lactate of 3.4 show a child compensating for blood loss, not a child who is truly well-perfused. The danger with pediatric shock is that kids hold their blood pressure until they can't — normal BP does not mean he is safe.

- **Compensatory mechanisms in children are powerful** and mask hypovolemia longer than in adults: his heart is racing and his body is squeezing blood away from skin and gut to keep his brain and heart perfused, which is why you see prolonged cap refill and mottled skin alongside a "normal" number.
- **Hepatic bleeding with falling hemoglobin** (now 9.8, down from baseline) is ongoing, and a blood pressure that was higher before the bolus but is drifting again suggests his intravascular volume is being outpaced by continued bleeding — the IV fluids bought time, not resolution.

Watch his trend: if his BP drops another 5–10 points or his cap refill exceeds 3 seconds, you've crossed from compensated to decompensated, and that is when you escalate — second bolus, typed and crossed blood standing by, and surgery moving to the OR.

vitals.label: SpO2
vitals.why:
SpO2 of 97% is reassuring right now, but it can hide a dangerous picture in trauma — Andres is breathing hard (RR 26, above the 18–25 norm for his age) and his lactate is climbing, which means his tissues are already oxygen-starved even though his lungs are moving oxygen into his blood just fine. Oxygenation (getting O2 into the blood) and perfusion (getting blood to the tissues) are two separate problems, and a normal SpO2 tells you only about the first one.

- **Respiratory compensation** for bleeding shock shows up as tachypnea and metabolic acidosis (rising lactate), not hypoxemia — the lungs are trying to buffer acidosis by blowing off CO2, and they're doing their job, so the SpO2 stays normal even as shock deepens.
- **Hemorrhagic shock in children** can mask itself with normal vital signs until suddenly it can't — normal BP, normal oxygen, but falling hemoglobin and rising lactate are the red flags that blood volume is draining faster than his body can compensate.

Keep the oxygen on, but your real focus is the bleeding source (hepatic laceration on CT), vascular access for packed cells and fluids, and the OR team on standby.

vitals.label: Temperature
vitals.why:
Temperature is reassuring here, and that matters because hypothermia in a bleeding child predicts worse outcomes. Andres is 37.3 °C — normal — which means his core temperature is holding despite significant blood loss and the early signs of shock (lactate 3.4, cap refill 4 seconds, climbing tachycardia). 

- **Compensatory mechanisms preserve core temperature** when perfusion is still adequate: vasoconstriction shunts blood away from the skin to vital organs, and metabolic rate stays up as catecholamines (the body's own adrenaline) surge. As long as those mechanisms work, core temperature stays normal.
- **Hypothermia in trauma signals late shock** — the body has exhausted its compensatory reserves and can no longer maintain heat despite active bleeding. Once temperature starts to drop, survival curves flatten sharply, especially in pediatric hemorrhage.

Watch the temperature closely during the next hour of resuscitation: if it begins to drift downward while you're running fluids and preparing for the OR, that's your signal that the bleeding is outpacing your ability to compensate, and surgery becomes emergent rather than urgent.

vitals.label: Cap Refill
vitals.why:
Cap refill of 4 seconds is markedly prolonged and signals that Andres's heart is struggling to push blood to his fingertips—a red flag for shock despite a blood pressure that still looks acceptable on paper. At 9 years old, cap refill should be ≤2 seconds; anything over 3 is abnormal, and 4 seconds paired with tachycardia, rising lactate, and a falling hemoglobin tells you his compensatory reserve is depleting fast.

- **Peripheral vasoconstriction** is the body's emergency squeeze to maintain central pressure when blood volume drops: catecholamines (his own adrenaline) clamp down arterioles in skin and extremities to shunt blood to the heart and brain, which is why you see both the slow refill and the pale, cool skin at the same time.
- **Hemorrhagic shock progression** moves from compensated (normal BP, fast HR, slow cap refill) to decompensated (falling BP, extreme HR, mottling, altered mental status) over minutes in a child—and Andres is in that compensated-but-sliding middle zone where the next bolus of fluid or transfusion becomes urgent.

This is the moment to escalate: push the second bolus, place a second IV line if possible, notify surgery, and watch for the point where BP begins to slip—that's your trigger to move toward OR.

signs.label: Mental Status
signs.finding: Alert and oriented, GCS 15. Increasingly anxious. No focal neurological deficits. Head CT result now available — no intracranial hemorrhage, no midline shift, no skull fracture. C-collar remains in place pending clinical clearance.
signs.why:
Andres is awake and thinking clearly right now, which is the good news — but his anxiety is the real signal you need to track. In hypovolemic shock from bleeding, mental status deteriorates in a specific sequence: anxiety first (the body senses falling perfusion before the brain shuts down), then lethargy, then confusion or unresponsiveness. He's at the early-warning stage.

- **Preserved orientation with rising anxiety** means his cerebral perfusion is still intact but his catecholamine surge is climbing — his body is fighting to keep blood flowing to the brain as his intravascular volume drops.
- **The combination of anxiety + tachycardia + tachypnea + prolonged cap refill + falling BP** tells you he's compensating hard right now, which buys time but not much; if bleeding continues unchecked, the anxiety will give way to lethargy within minutes.

His head CT clears traumatic brain injury, so you can anchor your concern where it belongs: on the abdominal bleeding and his need for urgent fluid resuscitation, CT imaging, and surgical evaluation.

signs.label: Abdomen
signs.finding: Right upper quadrant tenderness is now the dominant finding. Guarding is more pronounced on repeat exam. No frank peritoneal signs but trending in a concerning direction. Abdomen slightly more distended than on initial assessment.
signs.why:
Right upper quadrant tenderness that's worsening on repeat exam tells you the liver laceration is active bleeding, not contained — and the trend matters more than any single finding right now. Solid organ injuries bleed into the peritoneal cavity, and as blood accumulates, the visceral peritoneum stretches and produces focal tenderness and guarding at the site of injury.

- **Hemorrhagic shock from occult bleeding** is the working diagnosis here: his falling hemoglobin (9.8), rising lactate (3.4), prolonged cap refill (4 sec), and climbing tachycardia (138) all point to ongoing volume loss into the abdomen, and the worsening RUQ exam is the bedside confirmation that bleeding is not slowing down.
- **Peritoneal irritation progresses from tenderness to guarding to rigidity** as inflammation or blood volume builds; you're at the middle stage now, which is why surgery needs to know this is trending toward decompensation and may need operative control sooner rather than later.

Watch for peritoneal signs (true rigidity, rebound) or dropping mental status — either is an urgent trigger for immediate operative intervention.

signs.label: IV Access
signs.finding: Single 18-gauge right antecubital IV in place from arrival. No second IV access has been established. Given ongoing hemorrhage and potential surgical need, access is inadequate.
signs.why:
Andres has one IV in a peripheral arm vein with a child who's actively bleeding into his abdomen — that single line is not enough to keep up if his bleeding accelerates or if he needs urgent surgery. A pediatric trauma protocol in hemorrhagic shock demands at least two large-bore peripheral IVs or one peripheral plus central access, so you can run blood products, crystalloid, and colloid without getting bottlenecked when he needs it fastest.

- **Hemorrhagic shock resuscitation requires high-flow access:** a single 18-gauge line will deliver roughly 50–60 mL/min under gravity; two large-bore lines in parallel can deliver 200+ mL/min, which is the difference between keeping up with a slow bleed and falling behind a brisk one.
- **Surgical teams expect redundancy:** if he goes to the OR and that one IV infiltrates during transfer or induction, you've lost your access point when the surgeon needs to transfuse. A second IV or central line (femoral or subclavian, depending on your facility) gives you a backup and a way to push products faster than peripheral lines allow.

Place a second large-bore peripheral IV now, or escalate to a central line if peripheral access proves difficult — this is a "before the next crisis" intervention, not an elective one.

signs.label: Skin / Perfusion
signs.finding: Extremities cool to mid-forearm. Pallor worsening. Capillary refill remains 4 seconds peripherally.
signs.why:
Andres's cool extremities and 4-second capillary refill are the bedside language of inadequate perfusion — his body is rationing blood flow to the skin and periphery to preserve the heart and brain, and that trade-off only works until the tank runs dry. This is compensated hemorrhagic shock, but the compensation is fraying: his lactate is already 3.4 from tissue hypoxia, his hemoglobin has fallen to 9.8, and his BP is at threshold despite Round 1 fluids, so the next bolus needs to happen now.

- **Vasoconstriction** from catecholamines (the body's adrenaline surge) squeezes the skin vessels first, shunting blood centrally — cool skin and pallor are the visible cost of keeping his brain and heart perfused while he's bleeding into his belly.
- **Capillary refill ≥3 seconds** signals tissue perfusion pressure has dropped below the margin; combined with worsening pallor and a rising lactate, this tells you the compensatory squeeze is not keeping up with his blood loss any longer.

Push the second bolus without delay and have blood products ready for the operating room.

signs.label: Breath Sounds
signs.finding: Clear and equal bilaterally. Trachea midline. Splinting with deep breaths due to abdominal pain.
signs.why:
Clear and equal breath sounds with a midline trachea are reassuring — they tell you the airway is patent and ventilation is reaching both lungs evenly. In a trauma patient bleeding into the abdomen, this matters because it means you're not fighting a pneumothorax or hemothorax on top of hemorrhagic shock. The splinting you see (shallow breathing from abdominal pain) is expected after blunt abdominal trauma, not a sign of respiratory failure. His respiratory rate is elevated at 26 (above the school-age norm of 18–25), but that's compensation for the pain and the acidosis from his rising lactate — not primary lung injury.

- **Patent airway** stays his airway as long as mental status holds; you don't need to protect it yet, which frees you to focus on the bleeding source and vascular access.
- **Bilateral equal air entry** rules out tension physiology and lets you prioritize the abdomen; if either side suddenly quieted, that would be your signal to reassess for pneumothorax or tamponade.

Keep listening: if splinting worsens or breath sounds deteriorate, re-examine for a second injury hiding behind the obvious bleed.

labs.name: Hemoglobin
labs.why:
Andres's hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL tells you he has already lost enough blood volume that his oxygen-carrying capacity is dropping — this is not a lab artifact, it's evidence his bleeding is real and ongoing. A 9-year-old's baseline hemoglobin sits around 13–14 g/dL, so a fall below 10 signals significant blood loss, and the trajectory matters more than the single value: hemoglobin trends down during active hemorrhage and up during successful resuscitation or transfusion.

- **Acute blood loss lowers hemoglobin progressively.** Each milliliter of blood lost removes a proportional amount of hemoglobin; in trauma with a hepatic laceration, the bleed is continuing into the abdomen where you cannot see it, which is why his hemoglobin is falling despite the fluid bolus he's already received.
- **Low hemoglobin reduces oxygen delivery to tissues.** With a hemoglobin of 9.8, Andres's blood carries less oxygen per liter of plasma, and his tissues compensate by pulling harder — which is why his lactate is elevated and his capillary refill has stretched to 4 seconds despite a "normal" blood pressure.

If hemoglobin continues to fall or fails to respond to transfusion, prepare for operative hemorrhage control and massive transfusion protocol activation.

labs.name: Lactate
labs.why:
Andres's lactate of 3.4 is a warning that his tissues are not getting enough oxygen — his cells are switching to anaerobic metabolism and producing lactate as a byproduct, which means the bleeding is outpacing his body's ability to compensate on fluids alone.

- **Anaerobic glycolysis** occurs when oxygen delivery to tissues drops below their demand; without oxygen, cells burn glucose inefficiently and lactate accumulates as the end product, spilling into the bloodstream faster than the liver can clear it.
- **Shock compensation in children** relies on heart rate and vasoconstriction to maintain blood pressure, which masks the tissue-level oxygen crisis — his BP of 92/56 looks borderline acceptable, but the elevated lactate exposes what the vital sign is hiding: his tissues are already hypoxic.

Push the second bolus now, and if lactate climbs or fails to fall after resuscitation, he's telling you fluids alone won't stop the bleeding — surgery becomes urgent rather than elective.

labs.name: INR
labs.why:
INR of 1.3 means Andres's liver is beginning to falter under the shock load—his clotting factors are starting to lag, and that lag will accelerate if perfusion doesn't improve. This is an early warning that bleeding will become harder to control.

- **Hepatic synthesis of clotting factors (II, V, VII, X)** drops when liver perfusion fails; lactate rise and falling hemoglobin signal that shock is already stealing blood flow from the gut and liver. The INR creeps up because Factor VII has the shortest half-life and is the first to fall.
- **Coagulopathy in hemorrhagic shock** compounds the original bleed—Andres is losing RBCs AND losing the proteins that glue platelets together, which means each unit of blood he loses is harder to stanch. An INR of 1.3 is still mild, but it's the trajectory that matters: if shock deepens, INR will climb steeply and fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate will become necessary.

Watch the INR trend on the next lab draw (usually 1–2 hours); rising INR despite fluids and RBC transfusion is your signal that he needs massive transfusion protocol activation and operating room now, not later.

labs.name: ALT
labs.why:
ALT of 118 U/L signals acute hepatocellular injury — in this trauma patient with blunt abdominal impact and RUQ tenderness, it points directly to a hepatic laceration. The liver enzymes (ALT more than AST in acute injury) rise within minutes of parenchymal damage as hepatocytes spill their contents into the bloodstream; the magnitude doesn't predict bleeding severity, but the presence of a significantly elevated ALT in a hypotensive trauma patient with free fluid on ultrasound confirms the organ at risk.

- **Hepatic laceration mechanism:** blunt force ruptures hepatocyte membranes and disrupts the organ's architectural continuity, releasing intracellular transaminases and producing the bleeding cavity visible on eFAST and CT.
- **Lactate correlation:** his lactate of 3.4 with falling hemoglobin and slipping BP reflects ongoing blood loss into the peritoneum; the elevated transaminases confirm the source while lactate tracks his perfusion decompensation separate from liver function.

Watch for continued rise in ALT across repeated draws — static or dropping ALT in a patient with worsening shock suggests the bleeding has stopped or the liver injury is limited, while climbing ALT with worsening perfusion markers means the injury is expanding and surgical involvement is urgent.

labs.name: Potassium
labs.why:
Potassium of 4.3 is reassuringly normal right now, but it is a ticking clock in hemorrhagic shock — as resuscitation fluids dilute the serum and tissue perfusion improves, total body potassium deficit becomes visible and serum K+ can plummet dangerously. Watch it closely on repeat labs.

- **Dilutional hypokalemia** occurs as you pour in crystalloid and blood products: the ratio of potassium to total fluid volume drops, and serum K+ falls even though total body stores are already depleted from the injury itself.
- **Acidosis masking depleted stores** means the current normal K+ is misleading: acidosis shifts potassium out of cells into serum, artificially inflating the number; as perfusion improves and acidosis corrects, that buffering effect reverses and the deficit becomes apparent.

Recheck potassium after each round of resuscitation and before any blood transfusion, especially if the next labs show rising pH or falling lactate — those are the signals that correction is underway and hypokalemia is about to emerge.

labs.name: Creatinine
labs.why:
Andres's creatinine is reassuringly normal right now, but that's actually a narrow window — in hemorrhagic shock, creatinine rises late, after the kidneys have already been starved of blood for hours. The normal value tells you his renal perfusion is holding for now, but it's not a guarantee that he's safe.

- **Renal perfusion depends on adequate circulating volume.** Andres is bleeding into his abdomen with a falling hemoglobin and rising lactate; his kidneys are downstream of that hemorrhage, and once shock deepens, creatinine will climb as a sign that renal filtration is failing — by then minutes count.
- **Creatinine lags behind the hemodynamic injury.** A child can lose 20–30% of blood volume before blood pressure drops noticeably (they compensate beautifully), and renal function stays normal until perfusion truly fails — so a normal creatinine in early hemorrhagic shock is not reassurance, it's a green light to act before it turns red.

Keep rechecking creatinine every 2–4 hours; a rising value is your signal that volume resuscitation and surgery need to move faster.

abdomenCt.label: Order Abdominal CT with Contrast
abdomenCt.fb: Abdominal CT with contrast is the right call here because you need to know the exact location and grade of the hepatic laceration before deciding whether this bleeding stops on its own with fluids and time or demands the OR — and that decision changes everything about how aggressively you resuscitate. CT is fast, provides the anatomic roadmap surgery needs, and lets you triage between nonoperative management (for lower grades, which account for most pediatric blunt hepatic injuries) and operative intervention. While the CT is being acquired, keep two large-bore lines running, have O-neg blood in the bay, call surgery NOW so they're already thinking about this patient, and watch his serial labs and vitals — a rising lactate, falling hemoglobin, or worsening tachycardia despite fluids means the bleeding isn't slowing and you're moving to OR regardless of the CT grade. The scan answers the anatomy question; your resuscitation responsiveness answers the physiology question of whether he's actually hemorrhaging faster than he's compensating.

callSurgery.label: Activate Pediatric Surgery Consult
callSurgery.fb:
Andres is bleeding into his abdomen from a presumed hepatic laceration — his hemoglobin is falling, lactate is rising despite fluids, and his perfusion is worsening (cap refill now 4 seconds, tachycardia climbing). Surgery needs to be in the conversation now, not after CT results, because if he decompensates further you will need operative management within minutes and that coordination cannot start in the moment of crisis.

- **Damage control resuscitation in pediatric trauma** means fluid, blood products, and definitive hemorrhage control work in parallel, not sequence: while you're running the second bolus and getting ready to cross-match for pRBC, surgery is already mobilizing the OR team and reviewing imaging as it streams in.
- **Ongoing hemorrhage with declining compensation** (falling BP trend, climbing lactate despite resuscitation, deepening shock signs) is the trigger for surgical involvement — not wait-and-see, not "call when imaging is done." Early conversation lets surgery guide the pace of resuscitation and imaging, not react to decompensation.

This call buys time and coordination; it doesn't commit him to the OR, but it puts the team in motion if he needs them.

usGuidedPIV.label: Place Second Large-Bore IV (US-Guided)
usGuidedPIV.fb:
In hemorrhagic shock from a solid organ injury, you need two large-bore IVs — one is never enough when massive transfusion is a real possibility. Andres has one 18-gauge line already; the second large-bore IV is your redundancy and your speed if he begins to decompensate further or if the first line becomes compromised during transport to CT or the OR.

- **Hemorrhagic shock demands dual access** because crystalloid alone will not sustain him — blood products flow fastest through large-bore peripheral lines, and a single line forces you to choose between fluid resuscitation and ongoing assessment labs when minutes matter.
- **Ultrasound guidance bypasses the clock** when peripheral veins are harder to find after a 28 kg child has already burned one bolus; imaging the vein before you needle it saves time and saves the arm from repeat punctures in a child whose perfusion is already faltering.

Get the second line in before he rolls to CT, not after.

ioAccess.label: Place Intraosseous Access
ioAccess.fb:
IO access is the right call when you have one peripheral IV, falling hemoglobin, rising lactate, and a capillary refill stretched to 4 seconds — you need a second vascular lane right now, and you need it fast. Intraosseous needles place directly into the marrow space, bypassing the collapsed peripheral vasculature that shock creates; blood products and pressors infuse as reliably through IO as through central lines, and IO placement takes seconds while central line attempts eat critical minutes. Andres is compensating for now (alert, moving all four limbs, BP still at threshold) but his perfusion markers — the cap refill, the lactate, the falling hemoglobin — are sliding in the wrong direction, and a single IV is not enough margin if his bleeding declares itself further or if he needs rapid transfusion. A second access point in his tibia or humerus gives you the redundancy to keep up with his resuscitation.

- **Shock compensation is time-limited in children:** Andres is tachycardic and his cap refill is critically prolonged, which means his sympathetic nervous system is already squeezed to near-maximum. When that reserve runs out — and hepatic bleeding often runs it out fast — BP will drop suddenly; a second IV sitting unused is useless in the moment of crisis.
- **Intraosseous flow matches central line flow:** The marrow sinusoids drain directly to the central circulation, so medications and blood products reach the heart just as quickly through IO as through a femoral or subclavian line, with zero risk of tension pneumothorax or line placement delay.

Reassess his perfusion after Round 2 fluids and know where your IO kit is — if his cap refill doesn't improve or his tachycardia climbs further, you'll be inserting it under pressure.

vsMonitor.label: Confirm Continuous Vital Signs Monitoring
vsMonitor.fb: This was already set up in Round 1 and is still in place — repeating it now changes nothing for the patient. The evolved picture is asking for the next tier of care, not a repeat of the initial setup.

pocUltrasound.label: Repeat eFAST / POC Ultrasound
pocUltrasound.fb:
Repeat eFAST matters here because you need to know how much blood is in the abdomen right now — not just that it's there, but whether it's stable, growing, or declaring itself as an emergency. Andres has a focal hepatic injury with rising transaminases and worsening perfusion markers despite one fluid bolus; a second scan tells you whether the bleeding is slowing down or accelerating, which changes your next move from "resuscitate and transfer to OR" to "massive transfusion protocol and call for emergent anesthesia."

- **Serial eFAST quantifies bleeding trajectory.** Free fluid that remains stable or shrinks after fluid resuscitation suggests the bleed is self-limited or slowing; free fluid that grows tells you the liver injury is still active and you're losing the race against hemorrhage.
- **Hepatic lacerations often self-seal with volume support**, but you need imaging confirmation to bet your resuscitation strategy on that — a repeat scan showing stable fluid is permission to keep fluid resuscitating; growing fluid is permission to activate MTP and get surgical control.

Repeat the scan every 15–20 minutes in the bleeding trauma patient, or immediately if his perfusion worsens.

callBloodBank.label: Notify Blood Bank — Type and Crossmatch
callBloodBank.fb:
Notifying blood bank now is the right call because Andres is bleeding from his liver and already showing signs that his body is running out of compensatory room — a falling hemoglobin, rising lactate, slipping blood pressure, and cap refill of 4 seconds mean he needs blood products ready before he decompensates further. Type and crossmatch takes time; you don't have time once he declares himself. This is the moment to get ahead of the bleed.

- **Hemorrhagic shock compensation** relies on catecholamines squeezing blood away from skin and gut to keep the brain and heart perfused — his tachycardia, delayed cap refill, and elevated lactate tell you that squeeze is working but failing, and the next fluid bolus alone won't be enough.
- **Transfusion readiness** in pediatric trauma means the blood bank knows your patient's type before you need it; crossmatched PRBCs arrive in minutes rather than 30 minutes, which is the margin between controlled resuscitation and a child in extremis on your table.

Keep the collar in place and watch for any rise in abdominal distention, new vomiting, or worsening mental status — those are your signs the bleeding is outpacing resuscitation.

headOfBedElevation.label: Keep Head of Bed Flat (Hemorrhagic Shock Position)
headOfBedElevation.fb: Flat positioning is the right call for hemorrhagic shock from solid organ injury — but only after vascular access is secured and resuscitation is actively happening. Andres has one IV line and a rising lactate; the moment you lay him flat without a second large-bore access ready, you've lost your ability to infuse blood products fast enough if he decompensates further. Head-of-bed flat improves venous return to the heart by removing gravity's competition, which helps maintain preload when intravascular volume is depleted. In hemorrhagic shock from hepatic bleeding, flat positioning buys time for the bleeding to declare itself before you've committed him to a supine posture that limits airway access and makes rapid airway management harder if aspiration or respiratory decline occurs. Andres still has his airway, intact mental status, and time — secure a second large-bore IV (14 or 16 gauge, left arm preferred given the forearm fracture), confirm blood product availability at bedside, and notify surgery first. Once that package is in place, flat positioning + massive transfusion protocol becomes appropriate.

intubationKit.label: Prepare Intubation Kit
intubationKit.fb: Andres's airway is patent, his breathing is unlabored, and he's alert and answering questions — he needs his airway secured with vascular access and volume right now, not intubation. Intubation makes sense when a child loses the ability to protect the airway, when respiratory drive or oxygenation fails, or when rising intracranial pressure from head trauma demands sedation and controlled ventilation to protect from hypercapnia. Andres has none of those yet. His head CT is pending and his mental status is intact; the collar is doing its job. Preparing the kit pulls focus and personnel away from the hemorrhagic shock itself — two large-bore IVs, a second fluid bolus, and a call to the OR are what stop the bleeding spiral. Intubation without a clear airway indication in a bleeding child also risks losing spontaneous breathing, which means losing the patient's own drive to maintain minute ventilation while you're managing two simultaneous crises (airway and shock). Save the kit for the moment his mental status slips or his work of breathing rises — that's when you move.

lumbarPuncture.label: Perform Lumbar Puncture
lumbarPuncture.fb: This 9-year-old with head trauma and a scalp laceration needs imaging of that head injury first — a CT to rule out intracranial bleeding or swelling — not a lumbar puncture. A lumbar puncture is the right tool when you're testing cerebrospinal fluid for meningitis, encephalitis, or subarachnoid hemorrhage; it samples what's already in the spine. But Andres is actively bleeding into his belly from a likely liver laceration, his cap refill is 4 seconds, his lactate is climbing, and his blood pressure is slipping despite fluids. His mental status is intact and his head injury looks like a concussion with posttraumatic amnesia, not meningitis (no fever, no neck stiffness, no rash). Right now he needs a second IV access to keep up with hemorrhage, a stat abdominal CT to confirm the liver injury, and a call to surgery — not a procedure that takes time and carries a small risk of worsening intracranial pressure if there is any swelling. Save lumbar puncture for when you're worried about infection in the nervous system, not for trauma workup.

nsBolus.label: Administer NS Bolus 280 mL IV (10 mL/kg) — Re-dose
nsBolus.fb:
A second bolus of normal saline is the right move when a child re-bleeds or fails to compensate after the first round — this is the "re-dose" framework: reassess perfusion after each bolus, and if cap refill is still slow, skin is still mottled, and lactate is still rising, the tank is still empty and needs refilling before you reach for pressors.

- **Compensatory shock with ongoing hemorrhage** means Andres is using tachycardia and vasoconstriction to hold his BP at the low-normal threshold; a cap refill of 4 seconds and climbing lactate tell you those compensations are wearing thin and his intravascular volume has not caught up to his blood loss.
- **The 10 mL/kg bolus dose (280 mL here) matches pediatric trauma protocol** because it restores circulating volume without the risks of massive crystalloid that would dilute his clotting factors — you will pivot to pRBC and fresh frozen plasma soon, but right now isotonic fluid is the bridge that keeps him perfusing while CT and surgery coordinate.

Keep reassessing between boluses: if cap refill shortens and lactate stops climbing, the fluids are working; if cap refill stays ≥3 seconds and lactate continues rising, be ready to activate massive transfusion protocol.

prbc.label: Transfuse pRBCs 140 mL IV (~5 mL/kg)
prbc.fb: In hemorrhagic shock from solid-organ injury, blood products restore oxygen-carrying capacity and clotting factors simultaneously — crystalloid alone dilutes the very proteins he needs to stop bleeding. Andres has a falling hemoglobin (9.8 g/dL), rising lactate (3.4), slipping BP despite fluids, and focal RUQ tenderness with free fluid on ultrasound — the picture of active hepatic bleeding that fluids alone cannot reverse. A 5 mL/kg pRBC transfusion (~140 mL for his 28 kg weight) replaces lost hemoglobin and restores oxygen delivery to tissues while surgery is being mobilized. Packed red cells also contain residual plasma with clotting factors, and the elevated INR (1.3) signals early coagulopathy from dilution and consumption — pRBCs begin correcting both. Titrate to perfusion: watch cap refill, lactate trend, and BP response after each aliquot rather than hanging the whole volume at once.

tranexamicAcid.label: Administer Tranexamic Acid 280 mg IV (10 mg/kg) over 10 min
tranexamicAcid.fb:
Tranexamic acid (TXA) is the bleed-control drug in pediatric trauma within 3 hours of injury — it slows fibrin breakdown so clots stay intact longer, buying time for surgery to stop the bleeding at its source. Andres arrived from the field and is actively hemorrhaging into his abdomen from a likely hepatic laceration; his hemoglobin is already down to 9.8 and his lactate is climbing, which means his bleeding is outpacing his compensation. A 10 mg/kg bolus over 10 minutes (280 mg in his case at 28 kg) followed by an 8-hour infusion at 2 mg/kg/hr is the protocol supported by the CRASH-2 trial data adapted for pediatrics — timing matters because TXA's benefit disappears if given more than 3 hours after injury, and this child is still well within that window.

- **Antifibrinolysis** works by blocking plasminogen activation, which would otherwise dissolve the fibrin mesh holding clots together; in hemorrhagic shock where the bleeding site is still active, keeping clots stable long enough for the OR team to achieve surgical hemostasis makes the difference between salvage and decompensation.
- **Hepatic injury with rising transaminases and free fluid on eFAST** is exactly the picture where TXA prevents the secondary wave of coagulopathy — his INR is already creeping up and his RBC mass is dwindling, so the window to lock down clotting before he needs massive transfusion is closing fast.

Get the first bolus running now while CT is being done; his second IV will matter once he's in the OR.

fentanyl.label: Administer Fentanyl 14 mcg IV (0.5 mcg/kg) — Re-dose for Abdominal Pain
fentanyl.fb:
Pain control in a bleeding child keeps him from thrashing, splinting his belly, and worsening his own shock — fentanyl at 0.5 mcg/kg is the right dose for acute analgesia in trauma without oversedating him before the CT and surgery can assess what's happening inside.

- **Opioid analgesia preserves compensatory physiology:** Andres is tachycardic and cold-skinned because he's bleeding into his abdomen; pain adds sympathetic overdrive on top of that. Fentanyl quiets the pain without dropping his blood pressure the way deeper sedation would, letting his body's own catecholamine response (adrenaline) keep perfusion up while you're resuscitating the blood loss itself.
- **Dose-titering in hemorrhagic shock:** At 28 kg, 0.5 mcg/kg = 14 mcg IV — a modest dose that dulls pain without triggering respiratory depression or unresponsiveness. His cap refill is 4 seconds and lactate is climbing; he cannot afford CNS depression that masks deterioration or loosens his airway protection before surgery takes him.

Reassess pain and perfusion after each dose; if his mental status changes or his work of breathing rises, hold further opioid and call for help.

ondansetron.label: Administer Ondansetron 2.8 mg IV (0.1 mg/kg)
ondansetron.fb: Ondansetron blocks nausea and vomiting in a trauma patient bleeding into his abdomen — vomiting risks aspiration and raises intracranial pressure while your head CT is pending, and it causes fluid loss you cannot afford right now. Ondansetron is a **5-HT3 antagonist** that blocks serotonin receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and gut, shutting down the emetic reflex without sedating the patient or masking mental status changes. In Andres's case at 28 kg, 0.1 mg/kg gives 2.8 mg IV — a standard pediatric dose that works within 10–15 minutes and lasts 4+ hours. His **bleeding picture** (rising lactate, falling hemoglobin, hepatic injury on imaging) demands he stay NPO and keep his airway protected; nausea in this window is a threat to both. Give it now, before CT, before the next fluid push.

mannitol.label: Administer Mannitol 28 g IV (1 g/kg)
mannitol.fb:
Mannitol is the right call when raised intracranial pressure is the primary threat — head trauma with a blown pupil, impending herniation, or cerebral edema from DKA — but Andres's head injury is not the bleeding problem right now. Mannitol works by creating an osmotic gradient that pulls free water out of the brain parenchyma and into the intravascular space, which can temporarily lower ICP. His head CT is still pending and his mental status is intact; he's asking questions and following commands. The immediate life threat is hemorrhagic shock from the hepatic laceration, not cerebral swelling. Giving mannitol now pulls fluid from his already-depleted intravascular space into his urine, worsening the shock state when what he needs is fluid resuscitation and blood products to restore his circulating volume and oxygen-carrying capacity.

- **Osmotic diuretics worsen hypovolemia** by shifting fluid away from the vessels at the exact moment his BP is slipping and his lactate is climbing — both signs he's losing the race to maintain perfusion.
- **Head injury management priorities are sequential**: airway and breathing first, then hemorrhage control, then ICP management only after the head CT confirms significant injury and other causes of altered mental status are ruled out.

Hold mannitol until the head CT returns with a specific indication — until then, resuscitate the shock.

sodiumBicarb.label: Administer Sodium Bicarbonate IV
sodiumBicarb.fb:
Sodium bicarbonate is the right call when acidosis is driving cardiovascular collapse — cardiac arrhythmias from severe acidemia, or tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS widening — not in hemorrhagic shock with a borderline pH. Bicarbonate corrects acidosis by buffering hydrogen ions, which sounds like what a lactate of 3.4 should need. But Andres's lactate is elevated because tissue oxygen delivery has fallen behind demand from blood loss; his pH is still 7.28–7.32 range (mild acidosis, not severe). The real fix is volume replacement and transfusion to restore hemoglobin and cardiac output so his tissues can clear the lactate naturally as perfusion recovers. Bicarbonate here delays the actual intervention and can paradoxically worsen intracellular acidosis by generating CO2 that diffuses into cells faster than it leaves the bloodstream.

- **Hemorrhagic shock management** prioritizes red cell replacement and surgical hemostasis over pharmacologic buffer correction; fluids and blood products restore perfusion-driven lactate clearance.
- **Mild to moderate lactic acidosis** (pH >7.20) resolves as bleeding stops and oxygen delivery improves, making bicarbonate unnecessary and counterproductive.

ketamine.label: Administer Ketamine for Procedural Sedation/RSI
ketamine.fb: Andres needs airway protection and anesthesia for the abdominal CT scan — the right intervention from the sedation pack is a non-depolarizing agent like propofol or etomidate that preserves respiratory drive and airway reflexes without the cardiovascular hit he cannot afford right now. Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic that maintains spontaneous ventilation and airway tone, which sounds protective in general; it also has sympathomimetic properties that would normally preserve his blood pressure. But Andres is actively bleeding into his abdomen with a lactate of 3.4 and cap refill of 4 seconds — his catecholamine stores are already maxed out holding his BP near threshold. Ketamine's sympathomimetic effect relies on intact adrenergic reserves to work; in hypovolemic shock, those reserves are depleted, and ketamine becomes a direct myocardial depressant. A single dose risks dropping his already-borderline BP into frank hypotension exactly when you're losing intravascular volume. Propofol or etomidate gives you sedation without that cardiovascular gamble — etomidate especially preserves BP better in shock states.

emsReport: Medic 7 rolling in with Andres Villanueva, 9-year-old male, unrestrained fall approximately 10 feet from a treehouse onto mixed grass and dirt. He was found upright and crying at the scene. GCS was 14 at the scene, he opened eyes spontaneously, was confused and repeating himself, and withdrew to pain — he's improved to 14-15 en route and now he's verbally appropriate but still confused about what day it is. We collared him in the field for mechanism. Obvious angulated deformity of the left mid-forearm — we splinted it in place. Scalp lac over the left parietal region, actively bled at scene; we applied a pressure dressing and it's slowed way down. IV is in the right antecubital, 18-gauge, patent — no fluids hung yet. VS en route: HR 118, RR 22, BP 104/66, SpO2 97% on room air.
learnMore: Falls from height are the leading mechanism of pediatric trauma in the school-age group. A 10-foot fall carries enough kinetic energy to produce TBI, long-bone fractures, solid organ injury, and pneumothorax — even when the child appears to have 'landed okay.' The initial exam can dramatically underestimate injury burden; systematic primary and secondary surveys with low thresholds for imaging are the standard of care. Cervical spine injury after pediatric falls is uncommon but cannot be cleared clinically in a child who is confused or has distracting pain.

reassessment.narrative: After the second NS bolus and pRBC transfusion, Andres's heart rate comes down from 138 to 116 over about 15 minutes, and his capillary refill improves to 3 seconds. His abdominal CT confirms a Grade II hepatic laceration with a small perivascular hematoma and no active contrast extravasation — the bleeding appears to have slowed with resuscitation. Surgery is at the bedside and agrees with a non-operative management plan given hemodynamic response to transfusion and the absence of active extravasation on CT. His head CT (which returned during Phase 2) showed no intracranial pathology. Orthopedics has been notified about the left forearm deformity for definitive fixation once he is hemodynamically stable. TXA was given and blood bank has a crossmatch ready.
reassessment.stabilizationSummary: Andres is hemodynamically responding to resuscitation with a repeat hemoglobin pending and surgery monitoring closely for any deterioration requiring operative intervention. He's being transferred to the PICU for serial abdominal exams, hemodynamic monitoring, and ortho follow-up for his forearm fracture once stable. The collar will remain in place until a clinical cervical spine exam can be completed with the child fully cooperative and pain-free.

debrief.summary: Andres is a 9-year-old who sustained multisystem trauma from a 10-foot fall, presenting with a left forearm fracture, scalp laceration, retrograde amnesia, and occult solid organ injury that declared itself over the course of two rounds. His initial labs and eFAST gave early warning of hepatic injury, and the combination of rising lactate, falling hemoglobin, and evolving abdominal tenderness — despite an initial NS bolus and analgesia — correctly shifted the focus from pain management to hemorrhage control and surgical consultation. Early recognition of compensated hemorrhagic shock and timely escalation to transfusion and surgical input are the central teaching arcs of this case.
keyTeaching: In pediatric trauma, tachycardia that fails to improve after an initial fluid bolus should raise your index of suspicion for ongoing hemorrhage, even when blood pressure appears preserved.
An eFAST with free fluid in a child with abdominal tenderness and elevated liver enzymes is a hepatic laceration until proven otherwise — get the CT with contrast and call surgery early.
Compensated hemorrhagic shock in children is deceptive: BP can be maintained well into significant volume loss because of vigorous vasoconstriction — don't wait for hypotension to act.
Tranexamic acid (TXA) should be considered early in pediatric trauma with suspected or confirmed hemorrhage — evidence supports its use within 3 hours of injury for mortality benefit.
A single peripheral IV is inadequate for a child with ongoing hemorrhage — establishing a second large-bore line or intraosseous access before the patient decompensates is always the right move.

physiologyDeepDive.title: Hepatic Laceration and Hemorrhage in Pediatric Blunt Trauma
physiologyDeepDive.content:
In pediatric blunt trauma, the liver is the most commonly injured solid organ — it's large, fixed in the right upper quadrant, and has less protective musculature in children than in adults. A hepatic laceration can range from a tiny capsular tear that stops bleeding on its own to a major parenchymal injury with ongoing hemorrhage into the peritoneal cavity. The challenge is that children compensate brilliantly until they don't, so mild or moderate bleeding can hide behind normal vital signs for hours, and you have to read the other receipts — lactate, mild anemia, abdominal tenderness, liver enzyme rise — to catch it before shock.

- **The liver is 2–3% of body weight in children** (vs. 2% in adults) but proportionally more at risk because pediatric abdominal wall musculature is thinner and the rib cage is more pliable. A fall or motor vehicle impact that deflects rather than absorbs across an adult's ribs will transmit force directly to the liver capsule in a child.

- **Hepatic injury severity is graded I–VI** by the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST): Grade I is a subcapsular hematoma or small laceration; Grade VI is a hepatic avulsion (almost always fatal). In this scenario, Andres's mild elevation in ALT and AST (62 and 88 U/L) with trace hematuria and a lactate of 2.6 suggests Grade I–II injury — bleeding that's started but not massive.

- **Lactate is the receipt for tissue hypoxia**, and a lactate of 2.6 in a child with normal blood pressure and normal respiratory rate is the red flag that compensatory mechanisms are working hard. The child's HR is 122 and cap refill is 3 seconds — those are the child's way of saying "I'm losing blood volume" before the blood pressure drops.

- **The liver does not have a bare area; it bleeds into the peritoneal cavity, not retroperitoneally.** This means free fluid on ultrasound (eFAST) is the early sign. Peritoneal signs (rigidity, rebound, guarding) are late — they mean the child has hemorrhaged enough to irritate the peritoneum. Andres's soft abdomen with only mild diffuse tenderness is the classic early picture: bleeding is happening, but peritoneal irritation hasn't set in yet.

- **Blunt hepatic injury management is predominantly nonoperative in pediatrics.** Over 90% of pediatric liver injuries are managed without surgery — the goal is bed rest, serial exams, monitoring labs (Hgb trend, not just the first value), and watchful waiting in the ICU or high-acuity ward. Surgery is reserved for uncontrolled hemorrhage or peritoneal signs that persist despite resuscitation.

- **Resuscitation targets in pediatric blunt trauma differ from sepsis: permissive hypotension is no longer the standard.** Current PALS and AAP guidance recommend maintaining age-appropriate blood pressure and urine output (0.5–1 mL/kg/hr) with judicious crystalloid and early consideration of massive transfusion protocol if bleeding is active. The goal is oxygen delivery, not "keep the pressure low to avoid reopening clots."

- **Liver enzyme rise (transaminitis) lags behind the actual injury by hours.** ALT and AST can be normal immediately after injury, climb over the first 6–12 hours, and peak around day 2–3. The fact that Andres already has an AST of 88 and ALT of 62 in the ED tells you the injury happened some time ago (consistent with a fall from a treehouse where he lost 30 minutes of memory) and hepatocytes are leaking.

- **Ketamine and fentanyl are the preferred analgesics for suspected intra-abdominal injury** because they preserve airway reflexes and don't drop blood pressure acutely. Andres received both — fentanyl 1 mcg/kg and ketamine 0.5 mg/kg — because pain itself drives tachycardia and compensation, and controlling it reduces the work of bleeding.

- **Serial hemoglobin measurement is more predictive than a single value.** Andres's initial Hgb of 11.2 is mildly low for age (normal 11.5–15 g/dL in a 9-year-old boy), but it's the *trend* over the next 2–4 hours that tells you if bleeding is ongoing. A drop of >2 g/dL over 4 hours suggests continued hemorrhage and may trigger transfusion or escalation to ICU-level monitoring.

- **Head injury and abdominal injury often coexist in falls from height.** Andres has both a scalp laceration with anterograde amnesia (lost 30 minutes) and hepatic injury. The combination means close neuro checks (Glasgow Coma Score q15min initially), head CT before sedation if possible, and awareness that increasing intracranial pressure can worsen compensatory shock if the child's cerebral perfusion pressure drops.

**TL;DR:** Pediatric hepatic lacerations often hide behind normal vital signs because kids compensate so well — read the lactate, the liver enzymes, the cap refill, and the Hgb trend, not just the BP and HR. Most are managed nonoperatively with ICU-level observation, serial labs, and analgesia; surgery is for the child whose bleeding doesn't stop.

physiologyDeepDive.title: Compensated vs. Decompensated Hemorrhagic Shock in Children
physiologyDeepDive.content:
Andres is in compensated hemorrhagic shock—his body is holding his blood pressure up through tachycardia and vasoconstriction, but the cost is mounting. The distinction between compensated and decompensated shock is the difference between a child you catch in time and a child who crashes on your watch. In pediatrics, blood pressure stays normal until the very end, so you can't rely on it; instead, you read the signs of compensation—fast heart rate, cold skin, slow cap refill, metabolic acidosis—and act before the pressure drops.

- **Pediatric shock compensates longer than adult shock because children have better cardiac compliance and stronger sympathetic response.** A 9-year-old can maintain near-normal systolic pressure with 20–25% blood volume loss, but his heart rate and vasoconstriction are screaming "I'm bleeding." By contrast, an adult decompensates into hypotension much earlier with the same percent loss.

- **Tachycardia is the earliest, most sensitive sign of compensated hemorrhagic shock.** Andres's heart rate of 122–126 bpm in a 9-year-old (normal ~70–110) is his sympathetic nervous system maxing out norepinephrine and epinephrine.
